en: The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Gijjhakūṭa in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with twelve hundred [monks].
There were fifty bhikṣus present.
At that time, the King of Magadha, named Ajātaśatru, was at enmity with the kingdom of Vaiśālī and intended to go and attack it.
He consulted with his ministers, saying:

"The kingdom of Vaiśālī is wealthy, its people are numerous and flourishing, and it produces many rare treasures; since they have not submitted to me, would it not be appropriate to raise an army and attack their country?"
In the kingdom there was a worthy minister named Vassakāra. Minister Vassakāra was of the Ghoṭamukha clan, and he replied, "As you command.
The King spoke to Minister Vassakāra, saying:
"The Buddha is not far from here; if you take the King's word and go to where the Buddha is, bow your head at his feet and inquire after his well-being, asking whether his body is at peace."
"Are you eating as usual?
Having asked this and completed his prostrations to the Buddha, he spoke according to his own thoughts, saying to the Buddha:
"The King of Vaiśālī is arrogant and treats others with contempt; the King wishes to go and attack him. Will he be able to achieve victory?"

The Duke received the King’s command and immediately prepared five hundred chariots, two thousand cavalrymen, and two thousand infantry. He proceeded to the kingdom of Rājagṛha; having found a footpath, he dismounted from his carriage and went before the Buddha.
He bowed his head and face at the Buddha’s feet; the Buddha provided him with a stool and had him sit, then asked the Prime Minister of the kingdom, "From where have you come?
The official replied:
"The King has sent his minister here to bow his head at the Buddha's feet and inquire after the Buddha's well-being: 'Is your body in peace?
Is your food and drink as usual?
" The Buddha then asked:
"Is the King and the people of the state peaceful and harmonious?
Are the prices of grain low and stable?
The Duke replied:
"Having received the Buddha's grace, all have become peaceful and harmonious; the winds and rains are timely, and the kingdom is abundant.
The Buddha said, "Are the people, the roads, and the horses all safe and well?"
The Duke said,
"By receiving the Buddha's grace, I have practiced the Way and am entirely peaceful and free from harm.
The Duke addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The King has a grievance with the kingdom of Vaijayanta and wishes to go and destroy it;
what do you think of this, World-Honored One?
Will he be victorious? The Buddha said:
"If the people of the Vṛji kingdom uphold these seven dharmas, the king will not be able to defeat them; if they do not uphold these seven dharmas, they may be defeated.
The Buddha said, "In the past, I once went to the kingdom of Vṛji. There was a temple of the deity of swift action, and I stayed there for a while."
The elders of the kingdom of Vaiśālī all came and said to me:
"King Ajātaśatru intends to come and attack our country; we have strictly ordered ourselves to defend it."
The Buddha said:
"I have told the elders: do not grieve, do not fear;
if you uphold these seven dharmas, even if King Ajātaśatru comes, he will not be able to overcome you."
Vassakāra asked the Buddha,
"What are these seven dharmas?
At that time, the Buddha was seated, and Ānanda was fanning him from behind.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Have you not heard that the people of Vaiśālī frequently gather together to discuss matters of state and prepare for their own defense?"
He replied,
"I have heard that they gather together in great numbers to deliberate on matters of state and to prepare their defenses for self-preservation.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, he shall not decline.
Have you heard that in Vaiśālī, the ruler and his ministers are always in harmony, those they appoint are loyal and virtuous, and they continue to employ one another in succession?"
He replied, "I have heard that their ruler and ministers are always in harmony, and those they appoint are loyal and virtuous, succeeding one another in office. [The Buddha asked:
"Have you heard whether the kingdom of Vaṅga follows the Dharma in leading its people, being without grasping or craving, and not daring to commit transgressions?"
He replied, “I have heard that they uphold the Dharma and lead one another; they take nothing and desire nothing, and do not dare to commit transgressions. [The Buddha asked:
“Have you heard of the Yue-zhi? Are their rites and transformations reverent and respectful, such that there is distinction between men and women, and the elderly and the young serve one another?”
He replied, "I have heard that their rites and transformations are characterized by careful reverence; there is distinction between men and women, and the elderly and the young attend to one another.
"Have you heard of Yueqi? Are they filial toward their parents, deferential toward their elders and teachers, and do they receive admonitions and instruction?"
He replied, "I have heard that he is filial toward his parents, humble and respectful toward his teachers and elders, and accepts their admonitions and instructions.
[The King asked,] "Have you heard whether Yueqi honors Heaven and follows the patterns of Earth, reveres the altars of the land and grain, and serves the four seasons?"
He replied, “I have heard that he follows Heaven and obeys Earth, reveres the altars of soil and grain, and honors the four seasons. [The King asked:

“Have you heard of Yueqi? Does he honor and uphold the Way and its Virtue? When there are śramaṇas, arhats, or those who have come from afar in his kingdom, does he provide them with offerings of clothing, bedding, and medicine?”

He replied, "I have heard that he reveres the Way and its Virtue; whenever there are śramaṇas, arhats, or those who have come from afar in the land, he provides them with offerings of clothing, bedding, and medicine."
The Buddha said,
"For one who rules a kingdom, if these seven dharmas are practiced,
it will be difficult for them to fall into peril. Vṛṣa replied:
"If Yueqi were to uphold even a single precept, he would still be unassailable; how much more so if he upholds seven?
The Duke said, "State affairs are many and urgent; I must return to take my leave."
The Buddha said,
"You should know the proper time.
He then rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha called Ānanda and commanded him: "Go to Vulture Peak Mountain and invite all the bhikṣu-saṃgha to assemble together in the lecture hall."
Ānanda immediately accepted the instruction and went to Vulture Peak Mountain, where he addressed the community of bhikṣus:
"The Buddha invites the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus all came and paid homage to the Buddha. The Buddha then led the way to the lecture hall; once the seats had been prepared, they all sat down.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You all should uphold the seven rules of training.
What are these seven?
If bhikṣus frequently assemble to recite the sūtras, the Dharma will endure.
If those above and below succeed one another in their conduct of sitting and rising, the Dharma will endure.
If, while sitting or rising, they do not think of their households, wives, or children, the Dharma will endure.
Whether dwelling amidst mountain barriers, in deep forests, beneath trees, or among burial mounds, one should reflect upon the five conditions for the long endurance of the Dharma.

When young people embrace the Way, they should first consult elder bhikṣus, receiving their instructions with reverence and respect; by following their teachings without weariness, the Dharma may endure for a long time.
The mind should revere the Dharma and stand in awe of the sutras and precepts; thus the Dharma may endure for a long time.

By upholding the two hundred and fifty precepts in their entirety, one attains the path of Arhatship. Those who wish to come and study must not be turned away; those who enter shall follow one another’s example. Whatever clothing, bedding, food, or drink is possessed by those who come shall be shared in common, and the sick and frail shall be cared for by one another.
"If monks uphold these seven dharmas, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
"Furthermore, there are seven other dharmas; you may all listen.
The bhikṣus assented:
“I shall receive your instruction.
“A bhikṣu must not lie down in greed; while lying down, he must not think of other matters—thus the Dharma may endure.
He must delight in guarding purity and take no pleasure in conditioned things—thus the Dharma may endure.”
Delight in sitting together with the worthy, maintain the practice of forbearance, and be careful not to engage in disputes;
thus the Dharma may endure. Do not expect others to offer you reverence, and when preaching the sutras for others, do not regard it as a personal favor; thus the Dharma may endure.
Having attained the Way even slightly, do not allow yourself to become arrogant or unrestrained; thus may the Dharma endure.
Do not contemplate various sensual desires, and let your mind not incline toward other practices; for one who acts thus, the Dharma may endure.
Not coveting gain or offerings, always delighting in secluded places,
using a bed of grass as one's couch—
if a bhikṣu maintains this, the Dharma may endure for long.
“Furthermore, there are seven things that are all permitted.
The bhikṣus said: “We shall receive your instruction.”
"When a person bestows something upon another, others should not harbor resentment; thus the Dharma may endure long.
One should know shame and modesty; thus the Dharma may endure long.
One should not be lax regarding the sūtras and precepts; thus the Dharma may endure long."
If, whether sitting or rising, one does not forget the sutras and the Dharma, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
If, whether sitting or rising, one does not grow weary of or find it painful, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
If, whether sitting or rising, one clearly understands the sutras and the Dharma, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
When studying and reading the sutras, one should recite them while contemplating their profound meaning.
When a bhikṣu maintains these seven dharmas, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
Furthermore, there are another seven dharmas.
When the Buddha is in the world, he acts as the teacher for the bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus revere the precepts and instructions spoken by the Buddha, uphold and receive the dharma of the precepts, do not neglect the teacher’s kindness, and maintain the teacher’s dharma of precepts, then the Dharma will endure for a long time.
One must not deviate from the path; one should follow the constraints of the Buddha-dharma, and thus the Dharma may endure.
One should revere the community of bhikṣus and receive their instructions and precepts; one should accept and apply them without weariness, and thus the Dharma may endure.
When one reverently upholds the precepts and is able to practice forbearance, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
When one follows the sutras and precepts with a mind free from craving and attachment, and constantly reflects that human life is impermanent, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
During the day, one must not crave food; at night while lying down, one must not crave fine beds; in this way, the Dharma may endure for long.

One should admonish oneself to contemplate the world’s turmoil with constant mindfulness, never being indolent. Do not follow an evil mind, do not follow a deviant mind. When a deviant mind arises, restrain yourself and do not follow it; you should instead rectify your mind. People of the world are deceived by their own minds; as a bhikṣu, do not follow the minds of the foolish people of the world.
"By upholding these seven dharmas, the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Furthermore, there are another seven dharmas.
The bhikṣu-saṃgha said:
“I shall receive your instruction.

“A bhikṣu should revere the sūtras as a fool reveres precious jewels; he should regard the sūtras as his parents. He should live by means of the sūtras. While parents sustain a person for only one lifetime, the sūtras deliver people for countless lifetimes, enabling them to attain the path of Nirvāṇa. For this reason, the Dharma may endure for long.”

One must not greedily crave flavors; one must not eat excessively. To eat too much makes one ill, while eating too little leads to hunger; one should simply take what is sufficient. One must not seek the taste of the food; only then can the Dharma endure for a long time.

One should regard the body as being like the earth and constantly harbor anxiety regarding death; one should find no pleasure in the cycle of birth and death. Those who are born have much sorrow, grieving for parents, brothers, wives, children, relatives, servants, friends, livestock, fields, and houses. Such grief as these is all merely the grief of ignorance.
It is like a person who has committed a crime and is seized by an official; even if they have kinsmen, they cannot come forward to protect them because of that defilement.
One’s body should be compared to the earth: it comes alone and departs alone. Therefore, one should strive to master this body, for in this way the Dharma may endure.
Diligently cultivate vigor; keep the actions of body, speech, and mind upright and free from fault, and the attainment of the Way will not be difficult—the Dharma will endure.
Fearfully subdue the mind and its intentions, do not yield to the six sense-faculties, and suppress lust, anger, and delusion; being free from deviant conduct, the Dharma will endure.
Sitting among the multitude, he is not ashamed before them; he is respected by others because his mind is pure and upright, and thus he feels neither fear nor dread.

His pursuit of the Way is not crooked. It is like a person who has been slandered by others and arrested by officials; though the officials seize him, that person does not fear because he has committed no offense.
By maintaining pure precepts and revering the Buddha’s words of discipline, he sits among the multitude without fear; because his mind is pure, the Dharma shall endure for a long time.

One should be reverent and cautious, never being arrogant; one should receive the sutras and precepts from those possessed of wisdom, and when seeing those who are deluded, one should teach them the sutras and precepts.
When a bhikṣu upholds these seven dharmas, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
“Furthermore, there are seven dharmas.
The bhikṣu said,
“I shall receive the instruction.”

“A bhikṣu should constantly keep the sūtras in mind and cast off the disposition of lustful desire; he should constantly keep in mind the path that leads to transcendence of the world, and reflect upon his own body, for the Dharma is eternal.”

Constantly uphold the sutras spoken by the Buddha and keep them within your heart. Once they are kept within your heart, you should rectify your mind: discard evil thoughts and embrace wholesome ones. It is like a person whose clothes are heavily soiled; if they wash them repeatedly with strong lye, all the stains will eventually be removed.
You should remember the Buddha’s words, maintain the precepts, abandon evil, and pursue good; in this way, the Dharma may endure for a long time.

One should contend with the mind and not follow it; when the mind desires lust, anger, or delusion, one must not yield to them. One should always exercise self-restraint over the mind and not follow its impulses. It is like a person serving in an army: if one is a capable warrior, the multitude will all lead one forward to the vanguard of the ranks, making it difficult to retreat. Even if one wishes to regret and turn back, one feels ashamed before those behind. Having received the pure precepts, one should simply keep the mind upright and the intention correct, remaining at the forefront of the multitude rather than falling behind; thus one may attain the Way first, and the Dharma shall endure for long.

One should know the extent and depth of the dharma-practices one enters, and compare them with one's original resolve. One should daily delight in the sutras, neither wearying of suffering nor being choosy about food or bedding; by encouraging oneself through the Way, one finds joy, and the Dharma may endure for a long time.

One should respect one's fellow students and regard them as brothers; one should rectify both the external and the internal—the external being faults of body and speech, and the internal being faults of the mind. One should contemplate these two matters, for then the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Sitting in meditation, he reflected: "In these nine apertures, there is no foul discharge that is not present;

one aperture serves as the internal gateway, while all nine expel impurities. Hunger, satiety, cold, and heat are all extreme forms of suffering; the body finds it difficult to attain a state of comfort, for it is entirely unclean.

Impurity is harbored within, and when wind, cold, or heat manifest externally, this impurity turns back upon itself to cover them. When the nose perceives the expulsion of cold and heat, the mind is filled with displeasure; yet toward those things that have a foul odor, one feels neither aversion nor pleasure. A bhikṣu should rectify his mind regarding both the internal and external; in this way, the Dharma may endure for a long time."

When one observes all people in the world, even emperors and kings must die; whether poor or rich, noble or lowly, none can escape death. The way of life and death is the same for all: it is like a person who dreams of a magnificent house, a beautiful garden, and the pleasures of wealth and nobility, yet upon waking, sees them no more. All that exists in the world—poverty, wealth, nobility, and lowliness—is merely a dream, as when one reflects upon the world, it is just like a person's dream.
If a bhikṣu maintains these seven dharmas and reflects upon them without losing them, the Dharma will endure for a long time.
"Furthermore, there are seven other dharmas.

A bhikṣu-saṃgha should maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward the world and a mind of loving-kindness toward the Buddha. When reviled by others, one must not respond in kind nor harbor resentment; one should direct a mind of loving-kindness toward the world, just as those imprisoned within a jail always maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward one another."

When people dwell in this world, they should likewise maintain a heart of loving-kindness and take pity on one another. When a bhikṣu maintains his mind, he feels no anger when reviled by others; even when treated with contempt, he feels no joy. If such a mind arises, he can remain free from sorrow.

The reason one does not contend with worldly people is as follows: it is like a cow eating grass, from which milk is produced; from milk comes curd; from curd comes butter; and from butter is refined the finest cream (ghṛta). One should maintain the mind like this finest cream, upholding the Buddha’s precepts, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.

Keep the tongue upright and do not speak falsely; let your speech not wound the hearts of others. The tongue should be kept upright: if the tongue is not upright, it prevents people from attaining the Way.

The tongue brings forth swords and staves, or even leads to the destruction of one's entire clan. To practice the Way, one must always keep the tongue upright; thus the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Rectify your mind and do not think of evil; do not harbor thoughts of lust. One who possesses a lustful mind shall not achieve the path of an Arhat.
If, while lying down at night, the manifestations of sexual desire arise, you should contemplate the impurities of women, and the lustful intent will immediately dissolve.
If a heart of resentment and anger arises, you should contemplate that birth upon this earth is but brief, whereas the Dharma is enduring.
If someone is about to invite bhikṣus to a meal, others must not think, "This bhikṣu receives it alone; I do not receive it.
Such thoughts must not arise.
When a bhikṣu is ill, if someone happens to bring medicine for him out of a sense of duty, others must not think:
"He looks only after him and does not look after me."
One should not harbor such thoughts.
When someone presents clothing or other requisites to a bhikṣu, others must not think,
"Why have I alone not received them?"
Why is it that whatever is obtained through begging is acceptable?
Because it is placed within the alms bowl, one may not speak of its quantity; when the mind is thus, the Dharma can endure for long.
Uphold the Dharma of precepts and be cautious regarding the Dharma of precepts; those who do not know should inquire of bhikṣus who know the precepts.
Constantly recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus without ceasing, transmitting this practice from one to another.
If you find a louse within your robes, you should maintain a heart of compassion toward it; thus the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Seeing a dead person, he said:
"This person has already died; though his entire family weeps and his friends and relatives do not know, this person departs alone."

"A bhikṣu who has attained the Way is able to know the destination of the soul of a deceased person. One must not fail to read the Buddha’s sūtras, nor must one fail to study the Way. Among the many paths in the world, the royal road is the greatest; the Buddha-way is likewise so, for it is the supreme path."

It is like ten people, each holding a bow and arrows, shooting at a target; some hit it first, others hit it later, yet as long as they shoot without ceasing, they will inevitably hit the target again. Practicing the Way of the Buddha Sūtras is just like this: do not be indolent, and do not harbor distracting thoughts.

"In the past I attained the Way, yet now I have not attained the Way; I must harbor no resentment for this. Just as a person who shoots arrows does not cease until they hit the center of the target, so too, when a bhikṣu does not stop until he attains the Way, the Dharma will endure for a long time."

When sitting or rising, you should attend to one another; you should read, recite, and chant the Buddhist scriptures, and contemplate their meaning. With the exception of the *bhikṣuṇīs*, *upāsakas*, and *upāsikās*, these seven dharmas will ensure that the Teaching endures for a long time.
To uphold these forty-nine dharmas—seven times seven—is like the waters of the world: small streams flow into large streams, large streams flow into rivers, and rivers flow into the sea.
“Monks! Just as the waters flowing into the ocean do not cease until they meet it, so too shall you, by practicing the path without ceasing, attain the state of an Arhat.
The Buddha rose from Rājagṛha and called to Ānanda:
"Go to Pāṭaliputra.
Ānanda replied, "Yes."
He then traveled from the kingdom of Magadha before reaching Pāṭaliputra.
Along the way, there was a place called Rājagṛha; when the Buddha arrived there, he called to the community of bhikṣus:
"Listen all!"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:
“There are four sufferings in the world that the Buddha knows, yet which all people do not know.
Because people do not know them, birth and death do not cease, and there is no time of rest.”
What are these four?

They are the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death. Because people do not contemplate these four sufferings and endure them with forceful persistence, the cycle of birth and death continues without interruption or end. For this reason, the Buddha has proclaimed these four sufferings to inform humanity.
Although one has parents, wife, and children, all must eventually part; they will instead harbor mutual grief and lamentation without ceasing.

All manner of undesirable sights will appear daily before one’s eyes; for this reason, the Buddha has produced these scriptures: one should distance oneself from these four sufferings, observe the eight precepts, and regard even the body as something to be weary of.
The Buddha said:
"First, one must accept the words of the Buddha.
Second, one should distance oneself from craving and desire to pursue the Way, remaining free from greed and contention."
Third, one must not engage in false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, or harsh words; fourth, one must not kill, steal, or violate the wives of others;
fifth, one must not harbor envy, malice, or delusion.
Sixth, while sitting, one contemplates the four types of suffering, fixing the mind upon them.
Seventh, one reflects that the body is entirely impure.
Eighth, one observes that this body, subject to birth and death, will ultimately become nothing but dust.

The Buddhas of the past also contemplated these four sufferings; the Buddhas of the future will also contemplate these four sufferings. The Buddhas of the past also proclaimed these eight precepts; the Buddhas of the future will also proclaim these eight precepts. One should contemplate the profound meaning of the Buddha’s sutras.
"O Bhikṣus! Those who harbor thoughts of parents, wives, and children, and who are preoccupied with worldly livelihoods, shall not attain the path that transcends the world.

One whose mind delights in the world finds no joy in the Path; for the Path arises from the mind. One whose mind is upright may attain the Path; one whose mind is even if slightly so may ascend to heaven; one who clarifies the scriptures may become a human being. You must sever the paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."
"The Buddha has established the correct path for the cycle of birth and death for all under heaven; all bhikṣus should contemplate this.
From the village of Rājagṛha, the Buddha called Ānanda:
"Go to the village of Pāṭaligāma."
Ānanda replied,
“Yes,” and immediately followed the Buddha.
At that time, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus in the Saṃgha. When the Buddha arrived at the village of Bālaṇḍa, he sat beneath a tree.

The spirits and deities of the village of Bālaṇḍa immediately went to inform the Śreṣṭhin Śrīgupta; they all came forth, some carrying mats, some carrying grass seats, and some carrying lamps. They all proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him in homage, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha told Śreṇika Vatsagotra:
"When a person dwells in the world, if they harbor greed and abandon self-restraint, there are five evils.
What are these five?"
First, one's wealth and property diminish daily;
second, one does not understand the meaning of the Way;
third, one is not respected by others, and at the time of death, one feels regret.
Fourth, one will acquire an ugly reputation and an evil name that spreads far throughout the world.
Fifth, after death, one will enter the hells and the three evil realms.
If a person can subdue their mind and does not allow themselves to be self-indulgent, they will instead possess these five virtues.
What are the five?
First, one's wealth and property increase daily.
Second, one possesses the practice of the Path.
Third, one will be respected by the multitude and remain without regret until death.
Fourth, one’s good reputation and virtuous fame will be heard far and wide throughout the world.
Fifth, after death, one will be reborn in a place of superior merit and virtue.
"Do not be self-indulgent; these are the five virtues. You yourselves should reflect upon them.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra for the householder Śreṇika, they were all filled with joy, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
The Buddha rose and went to the village of Āveḷa, where he sat beneath a tree. With the eye of the Way, he beheld the higher devas and commanded the virtuous deities to protect this place.
Rising from his meditative seclusion, the Buddha departed from the village of Āveḷa and sat down in another location.
The venerable Ānanda adjusted his robes, rose from his seat, prostrated himself, and stood to one side.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Who is planning to establish a city wall and moat for this village of Pāṭaligāma?"
He replied,
"The Magadhan minister Vassakāra is planning to build this city, wishing to block off the Vṛjis.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Ānanda!
The noble Vappa Rāmagrāmaka truly knows how to plan this."

I have seen the various wondrous devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who together protect this land; wherever there is territory protected and sustained by the devas of heaven, that land will surely be peaceful and noble.
Furthermore, this land is the center of the heavens.

The deity who presides over these four regions is named Renyi (Benevolent Intent). Wherever Renyi provides protection, that nation will flourish and become increasingly superior over time; it will surely abound with sages, worthies, and those of wise counsel, such that other nations cannot equal it, nor can any destroy it.
When this city of Pāṭaliputra is about to be destroyed, it shall be by three things:
first, a great fire; second, a great flood; third, the inhabitants conspire with outsiders;
only then will this city be destroyed.

When the minister Vāsava heard that the Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus, had traveled from the kingdom of Magadha and arrived there, he immediately mounted five hundred state carriages of royal majesty and departed from the village of Pāṭaligāma for the place where the Buddha was. He went forward to pay homage to the Buddha, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha:
"Would it be possible for you to accept a light meal at my house tomorrow, together with the bhikṣus?"
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Venerable Vāsava spoke thus a second and a third time.
When the Buddha remains silent in the Dharma, it signifies as follows:

"Very well. Venerable Varṣākāra then departed, prepared the lodgings, and for the sake of the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, he arranged seats, lit lamps, and provided the requisites for food and drink.
The next day, Yushai Gong went to invite the Buddha. At that time, the Buddha went together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
When the meal was finished, the Buddha offered this blessing:

"May you attain the Way; do not take pleasure in the rank of a state official. Although in this life you cannot escape the jurisdiction of the government, because you have now fed the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, may you be liberated from the jurisdiction of the government in future lives."

In this world, those who possess wisdom should provide food for virtuous and good practitioners of the Way. When these practitioners offer prayers of blessing, one should not abandon official service; yet, in seeking office, one must not harbor greed, cruelty, ambition, delight, or the urge to promote oneself. If one serves as a local magistrate while setting aside these five matters, one may remain free from calamity and, after death, may be cleared of the sins that lead to hell.
"Venerable Yusha!
You should reflect upon this yourself.
The Master said:
"Very well, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha and the community of bhikṣus all rose and departed.
When the Buddha reached the city gate, the official followed behind the Buddha, intending to observe which city gate the Buddha exited through so that he might name it the "Buddha Gate."
The small stream he had crossed was named Buddha Creek.

When the Buddha reached the banks of the great river, many people and a vast multitude desired to cross; among them were some who traveled by large boats, some by small boats, and some by bamboo rafts. The Buddha sat down and reflected:
"Before I became a Buddha, when crossing this very water, I used bamboo rafts and boats to cross; now that I am the Buddha, my body shall no longer cross the water by means of bamboo rafts or boats."
The Buddha thought to himself:
"I am the teacher who delivers others; I shall cause people to attain the path that transcends the world, rather than receiving deliverance from others.
As soon as this thought arose, all the bhikṣus were already delivered.
The Buddha called to Ānanda,
"Let us go together to the village of Kauśāmbī. Ānanda said:
"So be it. The Buddha then, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, went as a whole to the village of Kauṇḍinya.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen all. Maintain a virtuous mind and do not contend with the world; reflect within yourself that you must understand impermanence, and use wisdom to take heed of the body.

Maintain a virtuous mind and do not contend with the world; reflect within yourself with immediate clarity. One who possesses clarity immediately abandons the states of greed, anger, and delusion. When these three states are abandoned, one attains the path to transcend the world, no longer subject to birth and death. The mind no longer wanders; it is single-mindedly without attachment, like a king who delights in solitary reflection, thinking: 'Among this multitude of people, I alone am the sovereign.'"

Those who have attained the Way and those who have crossed over the world likewise reflect upon their own minds, which possess many thousands of millions of facets; now all these are governed by this mind, just as a king presides over his people.
The Buddha again departed from the village of Kauṇḍinya and called Ānanda:
“Let us go together to the kingdom of Priyaka. Ānanda said:
“So be it. The Buddha, together with the bhikṣus, went to the kingdom of Priyaṅgu and sat beneath a kadamba tree.
The Buddha dispatched the community of bhikṣus to beg for alms throughout the kingdom of Priyaṅgu; having returned, they addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the kingdom of Xiyu, where many suffer from illness and many of the people die, there were ten lay followers (upāsakas)—named Xuānniǎo, Shíxiān, Chūdòng, Shìxián, Shūxián, Kuàixián, Bózōng, Jiānzūn, Dèjǔ, and Shàngjìng—all of whom were upāsakas who observed the five precepts; now they have all died."
The bhikṣus all asked the Buddha:
"To which realm do these upāsakas who have died all proceed?
The Buddha said:
"Xuan-niao and the other nine individuals have all died within the stage of the Non-returner (anāgāmin).
The Buddha told the assembly of bhikṣus:

"You all saw only these ten people die; however, when the Buddha perceives with his divine eye (divyacakṣus), he sees that five hundred upāsakas who have died have all been reborn in the stage of the Non-returner."

Furthermore, there were two hundred upāsakas, such as Nandiya and others, who at birth were free from lustful tendencies, free from angry tendencies, and free from deluded tendencies; upon death, they were all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, attained the stage of srotāpanna, and shall undergo seven more deaths and seven more births before attaining the path of arhatship.
The five hundred people, including Xuánniǎo and the others, all attained the stage of Non-returning (Anāgāmin), and they themselves shall attain the path of Arhatship (Arhat) in the heavens.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When you go out for alms and return, why do you ask about these ten upāsakas?”

If you wish to disturb the Buddha out of old habit, thinking that the Buddha does not wish to hear such evil, what fear or difficulty could the Buddha possibly have? All who are born must die; all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have entered parinirvāṇa.

Now that I have become a Buddha, I too shall enter parinirvāṇa. It is for this very body that I have become a Buddha; for many kalpas I sought Buddhahood, halting the path of birth and death. Having become a Buddha, I have severed the root of birth and death. I know that these beings originate from ignorance (*avidyā*); from ignorance comes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), from volitional formations comes consciousness (*vijñāna*), from consciousness come name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), from name-and-form come the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), from the six sense bases comes contact (*sparśa*), from contact comes feeling (*vedanā*), from feeling comes craving (*tṛṣṇā*), from craving comes clinging (*upādāna*), from clinging comes becoming (*bhava*), from becoming comes birth (*jāti*), and from birth come old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus, the great mass of suffering arises and accumulates.

The Buddha intentionally contemplated the root of birth and death: just as a chariot has wheels and the chariot moves without ceasing, so too does a person undergo birth and death because of delusion (*moha*). By removing delusion, delusion is extinguished; by the extinction of delusion, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are extinguished; by the extinction of volitional formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is extinguished; by the extinction of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is extinguished; by the extinction of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are extinguished; by the extinction of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) is extinguished; by the extinction of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) is extinguished; by the extinction of feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is extinguished; by the extinction of craving, clinging (*upādāna*) is extinguished; by the extinction of clinging, existence (*bhava*) is extinguished; by the extinction of existence, birth (*jāti*) is extinguished; by the extinction of birth, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are extinguished; and by the extinction of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are extinguished. In this way, the accumulation of the great aggregates (*skandha*) falls away and practice reaches its end.
The Buddha therefore previously taught you all that because of delusion there is birth and death, whereas the wise uphold the Way and no longer undergo birth and death.
The Buddha said:

“You all should mindfully honor the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the pure precepts; transmit one another the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures; and contemplate with a rectified mind so that you will no longer undergo birth and death, and be free from the suffering of grief and lamentation.”
The Buddha, departing from the village of Priya, called to Ānanda:
"Go to the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
Ānanda replied:
"So be it. The Buddha traveled from the village of Pāṭaligrāma to the kingdom of Vaiśālī; when he was seven *li* away from his destination, he halted at the Āmra Grove.

There was a courtesan named Āmrapālī who had five hundred female disciples. Hearing within the city that the Buddha had arrived and was staying in the Āmra Grove, she commanded her five hundred female disciples to dress themselves in fine garments and prepare their carriages. They departed from the city and went to where the Buddha was, desiring to see him and to prostrate before him.
At that time, the Buddha was in the Āmra Grove together with a thousand bhikṣus, preaching the sūtras to them.
Seeing the woman Āmrapālī accompanied by five hundred female attendants, all beautifully adorned in their garments, the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus:

"When you see the woman Āmrapālī and her five hundred female attendants, all of you lower your heads and maintain a focused mind. Although they come beautifully adorned, they are like painted vases: though there are fine paintings on the outside, inside there is only impurity. It is sealed shut and cannot be opened; were it opened, the foul stench would immediately emerge."
These women are all of the same sort as the jars; a bhikṣu must possess the power of vision. What is meant by the power of vision?

It is to abandon evil and pursue good, and not to indulge in lewd conduct. One would rather break one's own bones, shatter one's heart, and burn one's body than ever follow the mind to commit evil. It is not merely the strong man who possesses great strength; one who can rectify their own mind surpasses the strong man.
Since the Buddha has contended with his own mind for incalculable eons, he did not allow himself to follow the mind, but through diligent effort and perseverance, he attained Buddhahood by himself.

Monks, you should likewise rectify and align your own minds. For a long time the mind has dwelt amidst impurity; now it must be extricated. Contemplate the five viscera within your own bodies, and likewise bring to rest the phenomena of birth and death. View the external as suffering and view the internal as suffering; keep your mind upright.

When the daughter of Nyagrodha arrived, she alighted from her carriage and approached the Buddha; she paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to sit on one side, while all the bhikṣus lowered their heads.
The Buddha asked, "For what reason have you come?"
The daughter of the Nyagrodha tree said, "I have often heard that the Buddha is more venerable than all the devas; therefore, I have come to kneel and pay my respects.
The Buddha said:
“Nanda, do you delight in being a woman? Nanda replied:
“I have merely been made a woman by Heaven; I do not delight in this.
The Buddha said, “If you do not delight in being a woman, who compelled you to maintain five hundred lustful disciples?”
The daughter of Nyagrodha said,
"These are all poor people whom I support and protect.
The Buddha said:

"Not so. If you do not grow weary of the afflictions of womanhood—the impurity of the monthly courses, the shackles and the blows, and the lack of autonomy—and if you do not grow weary of your own body, why instead follow five hundred men?"
The daughter of Nanda said, "This was due to my ignorance; a wise person would not do such a thing.
The Buddha said:
"It is well that you have examined it thus.
The maiden then knelt upright and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for tomorrow."
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
The daughter of the Āmra tree was greatly delighted; she immediately rose, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.

Not long after she had left, the wealthy householders of Vaiśālī heard that the Buddha and his community of bhikṣus had arrived together and were staying seven *li* from the city within the Āmra grove.
Taking advantage of the King’s majesty, they all prepared their carriages and set forth, desiring to have an audience with and make offerings to the Buddha.
Among them, some rode on blue horses and blue chariots, with blue robes, blue canopies, blue banners, and blue streamers; their entire retinues were likewise blue.
Others rode on yellow horses and yellow chariots, with yellow robes, yellow canopies, yellow banners, and yellow streamers; their entire retinues were likewise yellow.
Among them, some ride red horses and red chariots, with red garments and red canopies, red banners and red pennants, and their entire retinues are red;
some ride white horses and white chariots, with white garments and white canopies, white banners and white pennants, and their entire retinues are white;
others ride black horses and black chariots, with black garments and black canopies, black banners and black pennants, and their entire retinues are black.
The Buddha saw from afar a procession of several hundred thousand chariots and horsemen approaching, and he immediately addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to see the attendants entering and exiting the celestial gardens of Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they are no different from these householders."

When the householders reached the entrance of the gate, they all alighted from their carriages and proceeded to where the Buddha was. Those in front knelt before the Buddha; those in the middle bowed their heads; and those at the rear simply joined their palms and sat down.
The Buddha asked,
"From where have you all come?
The householders replied:
"Because we have heard that the Buddha is here, we have come out of the city to prostrate ourselves.
Among them was one man named Binzi, who rose and went before the Buddha, gazing intently at him.
The Buddha asked,
"How do you regard it? Bin replied:
"From the heavens above to the earth below, all are stirred by the Buddha; I behold the Buddha without ever reaching satiety.
The Buddha said, "Bimbisāra!"
Zhuang should gaze intently at the Buddha; it will be only after a long time that another Buddha appears again, and while there is a Buddha, one must receive his teachings and commands.
Among them, four or five hundred householders said, “The guest himself possesses great virtue; let him converse with the Buddha.”
The guest said of himself:

"I have heard the Buddha’s sutras from afar; I have long cherished the thought of practicing according to these sutras, and it is only today that I have finally been able to see them. I possess a heart of compassionate filiality toward the Buddha."
The Buddha said, "In all the world,
there are few who are like Binzi, showing such loving-kindness and filial piety toward their teacher.
The Buddha then addressed Binzi:

“The Buddha has appeared in the world and understands the way of birth and death in the world; he preaches the sutras to transform those in heaven above and the world below, as well as the ghosts and dragons, such that there are none who do not bow in reverence—this is the Buddha’s first majestic spiritual power.”
That there are those who read the Buddha’s sutras, rectify their own minds, and attain the Way—this is the second majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.

When the Buddha preaches the sutras throughout the world, there are no sages who do not rejoice, and no hearers who do not rejoice; those who study them teach one another, instruct one another, and rectify one another's minds—this is the third majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.

Those who study the Buddhist scriptures all rejoice, like a fool who finds gold. The highest wise person attains the path of Arhatship (Skt. *arhat*); the second may attain the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*); the third may attain the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*); the fourth may attain the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Fifth, those who uphold the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) may go to the heavens; those who uphold the three precepts may become human beings again.
"The Buddha has appeared in the world and manifested this path; this is the fourth majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Pindola:
"If you come and gaze intently upon the Buddha, or if you speak of him, you have heard the Buddha's name many times, yet it is rare to actually behold the Buddha."

At that time, there were several hundred thousand people sitting in the assembly, none of whom questioned the Buddha except for this one individual; this was the fifth of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual powers. The Buddha told Binzi: "In the world, those with wisdom are few, while those who lack gratitude and reciprocity are many.

When one receives the Buddha’s sutras and the Way, accepts the teacher’s kind words, and upholds the teacher’s precepts and Dharma, there are no ghosts, spirits, or dragons who will not protect and watch over them. Even officials dare not summon them recklessly. One should be compassionate and filial toward the teacher; while before the teacher, one should show respect, and behind the teacher’s back, one should praise them. After the teacher has passed away, one should always remember them. As for Binzi here today, he is a hero among men, delighting in the Dharma and pure in his precepts."
The Śākyan householder of Vaiśālī invited the Buddha for the following morning, saying, "Would you be so kind as to enter the city with the bhikṣus for a meal?
The Buddha said,
"The daughter of Nyagrodha has come this morning to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
The various *tīrthikas* and practitioners of mental cultivation all departed together.
On the following morning, the maiden Āmrapālī came to the Buddha’s dwelling and addressed him, saying:
“The seats have been prepared and the provisions for the meal are all ready; I pray that the World-Honored One will deign to manifest his majestic power.”
The Buddha said,
"If you go directly ahead, I shall follow behind.
The Buddha rose, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city together with the bhikṣu.
There were several hundred thousand spectators in the city, among whom was a virtuous and noble upāsaka who said:
"The Buddha is like the bright moon, and his disciples are like the lesser stars that follow it."
At that time, the Buddha was pleased with this.

When the Buddha arrived at the house of the woman from the Āmra grove, he took his seat and water for washing was served. After the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus had finished their meal and the washing of hands was completed, the woman from the Āmra grove took a small stool and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha told the daughter of Māṇava:
"The sages and the most honored, noble, wealthy, and powerful in the world value only the purity of the precepts and clarify the various sutras of the Buddha.

Their speech within the assembly is never unpleasant to hear, and wherever they go, there are none who do not revere and love them. Now, among the people of the world, those who do not covet wealth or beauty and who uphold the divine transformation of the Buddha will, upon death, all be reborn in the heavens."
The Buddha told the girl Nanda:
"Take good care of yourself and observe the five precepts.
Then the Buddha departed together with the bhikṣus.
The Buddha departed from the kingdom of Vaiśālī and addressed Ānanda:
"It would be well for us both to go together to the village of Veṇugrāmaka. Ānanda said:
"Yes," [they replied].
Furthermore, they heard that in the village of Zhufang, rice and grain were extremely expensive, making it difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain alms through their begging rounds.

The Buddha sat in contemplation, reflecting that the kingdom of Vaiśālī was suffering from famine and the price of grain had soared; moreover, that settlement was small and could not provide for the bhikṣus' alms-gathering. The Buddha thought of sending the bhikṣus to various other countries where rice and grain were cheap to go on their begging rounds.
The Buddha told the community of bhikṣus:
"In this village of Zhufang, rice and grain have soared in price, making it difficult to obtain alms;
however, in that region there is the country of Śaradvatī, where the harvests are abundant."
"In this city of Vaiśālī, the four elements are in turmoil and rice and grain are all expensive; I shall stay here with Ānanda at this Bamboo Grove.
The bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, all departed for the country of Sālāthi.
The Buddha, accompanied by Ānanda, arrived at the village of Veṇugrāmaka; his body was in great pain, and he desired to enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"All the bhikṣus have departed, yet I alone am entering parinirvāṇa—would this not be improper, lacking instruction and precepts?"
Ānanda rose from beneath a tree, went to where the Buddha was, and asked the Buddha:
"Is your holy body not feeling well? Has it not improved?
The Buddha said:
“I am not yet free from great illness; I wish to enter parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda said, “Do not enter parinirvāṇa yet; you must wait for the assembly of bhikṣus to gather.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: "I already possess the sūtras and the precepts; you all should simply follow and practice them according to the sūtras and the precepts. I am also among the community of bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus all know the instructions of the Buddha. The methods for serving a teacher have all been entrusted to the disciples; the disciples should simply uphold and practice them, studying them thoroughly."

"Now my body is entirely in pain; I am treating this illness by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, no longer using my own mind to contemplate the disease, as if it were a slight recovery.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Now the Buddha’s years are already advanced, being nearly eighty;

like an old cart that lacks strength and durability, my physical body is likewise without strength or durability. Originally, I did not speak for you all, saying that there is none who falls to the ground and does not die, for even the highest heaven, named Asaṃjñisattva (The Unconscious), has a lifespan of eighty-four billion kalpas, yet they too must eventually die. For this reason, I have raised up this scripture throughout the world to sever the very root of birth and death."

After my parinirvāṇa, you must not abandon these sutras and precepts; transmit and employ them to one another. Reflecting upon both the internal and external, keep your minds upright and your conduct correct. You should uphold the dharma of the precepts, ensuring that both the internal and external remain as they have always been.
Among those four classes of disciples, all who uphold the Dharma of the precepts are disciples of the Buddha; all who study the path of the Buddha’s sutras are disciples of the Buddha.

The Buddha, having renounced the status of a Wheel-Turning King, felt concern for those above and below in heaven and earth; he likewise took concern for his own illness and exhorted [his disciples] to abandon lustful states, angry states, and deluded states.
Departing from Bamboo Grove, the Buddha called to Ānanda:
"Let us return once more to the kingdom of Vaiśālī."
Ānanda replied, “I shall receive your instructions.

The Buddha returned to the kingdom of Vaiśālī; entering the city with his almsbowl, he went on his rounds for alms and then returned to sit in the open air beneath the Ajapāla tree, contemplating the matters of birth and death.

Ānanda was at a distance beneath a tree, contemplating matters concerning the chamber of the five aggregates. He rose and went to where the Buddha was; having paid homage to the Buddha, he stood before him and said to the Buddha:
"Why do you not enter parinirvāṇa?"

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Vaiśālī is a place of great joy; Vārāṇasī is a place of great joy; the land of the swift deities is a place of great joy; the city gate of Śrāvastī is a place of great joy; the streets and alleys within the city are places of great joy; the marketplace of Campā is a place of great joy; Jambudvīpa is a place of great joy; Vajjī is a place of great joy; the kingdom of Campa is a place of great joy; the city gate of Sāketa is a place of great joy; Magadha is a place of great joy; Pāṭaliputra is a place of great joy; Ujjayinī is a place of great joy; the Golden Mountain where the Haimavatī River flows is a place of great joy; and within the interior of Jambudvīpa, where the five colors appear like a painting, those born therein experience great joy.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who uphold these four dharmas, reflecting deeply with a rectified mind and not following after their own impulses, contemplating what is wholesome externally and what is wholesome internally, and whose minds no longer harbor further craving or delight, nor are they startled or terrified, nor do they run away—those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who maintain such a resolute intention through these four dharmas are said to possess the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*). If they so desire, they may remain for an entire eon without dying."
At that time, Māra entered Ānanda’s belly.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
“Even this is still permissible.”
Ānanda spoke again:
"Why does the Buddha not enter parinirvāṇa?
The time is now fit for him to enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha spoke again:
"Jambudvīpa is a great joy; whoever knows these four bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) shall be able to remain within the world for more than one kalpa."
The Buddha addressed Ānanda thus, repeating it a second and a third time, yet Ānanda did not respond to the matter of the four bases of psychic power.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Go back and reflect upon this yourself beneath the tree."
The Buddha rose and went to the bank of the Hiraṇyavatī River, where he sat beneath a tree. Māra came to where the Buddha was and said, "Why do you not enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha replied:
"Ha! Wretched Māra! You must not enter parinirvāṇa yet.

You must wait until my fourfold assembly of disciples have attained the Way through their keen wisdom; you must wait until the gods of the heavens and the people of the world, down to the ghosts and spirits, have attained the Way through their wisdom; you must wait until my sūtras and Dharma have spread throughout the world—only then may you enter parinirvāṇa."
Knowing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Māra departed with joy.
The Buddha sat in contemplation, thinking to himself:
"I may now relinquish my life-force; I intend to relinquish my life-force."
At that time, heaven and earth shook violently, and all the spirits and deities were struck with alarm.
Ānanda, sitting beneath a tree, rose in startled haste to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself before the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha:
“While I was sitting beneath the tree, heaven and earth shook violently. I was so startled that my hair stood on end; in all my life, I have never experienced such a trembling of the earth.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There are eight causes by which heaven and earth tremble. What are these eight?"

The earth rests upon the water, and the water rests upon the wind; the wind sustains the water, just as one looks toward the sky from the surface of the earth. Sometimes the wind moves the water, the water moves the earth, and the earth consequently shakes—this constitutes the first movement.

There was an Arhat of noble status who, wishing to test his own spiritual power and desiring to cause the earth to tremble, pressed down on the ground with two fingers of his hand; consequently, heaven and earth shook violently—this constitutes the second trembling.
Among them, there are devas of great majestic power who, when they desire to move the earth, the earth immediately shakes violently; this is the third shaking.
Furthermore, when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, descending from the fourth Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, at that time heaven and earth shook violently.
When the Bodhisattva was born from the right side, heaven and earth shook greatly.
When the Bodhisattva attained the Way and became a Buddha, heaven and earth shook greatly.
When the Buddha arose from his original seat and preached the sutra, heaven and earth shook greatly.
"When the Buddha relinquishes his life-span, heaven and earth undergo a great trembling.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Now, three months from now, the Buddha shall enter parinirvāṇa; heaven and earth shall again undergo a great trembling—this constitutes the eighth trembling."
When Ānanda heard that the Buddha had personally pledged three months [of seclusion], he wept and asked,
"Is it not that you intend to cast away your life-span?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Therefore, one abandons the life-span.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have heard and received this directly from the Buddha's own mouth: 'If a bhikṣu possesses these four dharmas, which are called the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), he may, if he so desires, remain for an entire eon without dying.'"
“The Buddha’s virtue exceeds the four bases of psychic power; why then does he not remain for more than one kalpa?
The Buddha told Ānanda: “This is as it is; this is what you have done.”
I have entreated you repeatedly, saying that within Jambudvīpa there is great happiness;
yet you remain silent and do not respond.
I see your horns—how is it that you allow Māra to enter into your belly?
"I can no longer remain; three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda immediately rose and addressed the community of bhikṣus:
"The Buddha will enter parinirvāṇa three months from now."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Gather all the bhikṣus together and bring them into the Great Assembly Hall.
Ānanda replied:
"The community of bhikṣus is all gathered in the Great Assembly Hall.
The Buddha immediately rose and proceeded to the Great Assembly Hall; the bhikṣus all rose and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In this world, those who lack constancy and firmness, who delight in birth and death, and who do not seek the path to transcend the world—all such people are deluded."

Parents must all eventually part, giving rise to thoughts of grief and weeping; as people turn toward one another with affection, longing, and sorrow, there is no one in the world who is born and does not die.
In my original sutras I have taught that all who are born must die, and those who die are reborn again, weeping for one another without ceasing.

Even Mount Sumeru shall crumble, and the gods in heaven also die; even those who rule as kings die. From the poor, the wealthy, the noble, and the lowly, down to the animals—there is no one born who does not die. Do not be surprised that the Buddha will enter parinirvāṇa three months from now.

Whether the Buddha has departed, one should uphold the sutras and precepts; whether he remains present, one should likewise uphold the sutras and precepts. Thus one shall proceed toward transcendence of the world, no longer subject to birth and death, and forever free from sorrow and weeping.

The Buddha’s sutras shall endure for a long time; after the Buddha has passed away, the wise ones of the world should together uphold the sutras and the precepts. For those people of the world who rectify their own minds, all the devas in the heavens will rejoice and assist them so that they may obtain blessings.
The Buddhist scriptures may be read, recited, studied, upheld, contemplated, used to rectify the heart, used to align the mind, and used to instruct one another; there are four matters for this:
rectifying the body, rectifying the heart, rectifying the will, and rectifying the speech.

Furthermore, there are four matters: one who is prone to anger should practice patience; one with evil thoughts should abandon them; one with covetous desires should abandon them; and one should always be mindful of death. Again, there are four matters:

do not allow the mind to incline toward deviance; do not allow the mind to incline toward lust; do not allow the mind to contemplate what is evil; and do not allow the mind to contemplate wealth and nobility.

Furthermore, there are four matters: one should always be mindful of death; one must not permit the mind to plot evil; one should restrain the mind; and the mind should follow the person, rather than the person following the mind. The mind deceives people; the mind kills the body; the mind attains the state of an Arhat; the mind attains heaven; the mind attains the human realm; the mind attains the states of animals, insects, ants, birds, and beasts; the mind attains hell; and the mind attains the realm of hungry ghosts. Those who assume physical forms are all created by the mind.

Life-span, the third, follows these two; the mind is the foremost teacher. Life follows the mind, and life-span follows life; these three follow one another. Now that I have become a Buddha and am honored by those above and below in heaven and earth, it is all due to what the mind has accomplished. You should contemplate the suffering of birth and death and the separation from one’s family; you should contemplate these eight matters and reflect upon the Buddhist sutras:
First, one should abandon wife and children to seek the path to transcendence, not contend with the world, and be free from greed.
Second, one must not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, or frivolous talk, nor indulge in whistling, singing, or playful dalliance.
Third, one must not kill living beings, steal another's property, or harbor thoughts of sexual lust.
Fourth, one must not harbor anger, delusion, or greed.
Fifth, one must not be envious of others or be arrogant toward them.
Sixth, one must not contemplate committing evil or inflicting suffering upon others.
Seventh, one must not display affectations or assume an air of self-importance; one must not be indolent or addicted to reclining, nor should one be attached to the flavors of food and drink.
Eighth, one should take concern for the body’s birth, aging, sickness, and death.
By upholding these eight matters, one rectifies one's own mind and may remain without contention with the world, proceeding toward the path that transcends the world.
"Monks, you should contemplate these eight matters; when the four types of sensation are understood, the Buddha's teaching will endure for a long time.
From the country of Vaiśālī, the Buddha called Ānanda:
"Go to the village of Kuṇḍala."
Ānanda replied,
“Yes. The Buddha departed from the city of Vaiśālī and turned his body to look back at the city.
Ānanda immediately stepped forward and asked the Buddha,
"The Buddha does not turn his body to look at the city without purpose.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I do not turn my body in vain; indeed, when one acts as a Buddha, one must not turn back to look.
Ānanda asked:
"What is the meaning of the Buddha turning back to look?"
The Buddha said, "My life today has reached its end; I shall not enter this city again, which is why I have looked back.
A bhikṣu who was following the Buddha stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
“Will you not return to this city now? The Buddha said, “I shall enter parinirvāṇa;
I shall not see the kingdom of Vaiśālī again, but shall go to the land of Pāṭaliputra.”
The Buddha arrived at the village of Kuṇḍi. In that village there was a park named Śiśumāra. The Buddha called out to all the bhikṣus:

"Now sit with pure and clean minds and reflect within yourselves. Those who possess wisdom within their lives shall make their minds upright. When the mind is upright, the three states of lust, anger, and delusion are all liberated. Such a bhikṣu may declare for himself that he has severed the root of birth and death and attained the path of Arhatship. With a single-minded focus free from further anxiety, he no longer grieves over birth and death; though he undergoes further suffering, he has attained the path beyond birth and death."
The Buddha, departing from the village of Kauṇḍinya, called to Ānanda:
"Go to the village of Kāli.
Ānanda said:
"So be it. The Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus, arrived at the village of Kāli.
From the village of Kāli, the Buddha called to Ānanda:
“Let us all go to the heap of gold.
Together with the community of bhikṣus, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there is a bhikṣu who, with a pure mind, a mind of wisdom, and a mind of self-reflection, possesses the knowledge of the sūtras, this is the root of the mind of insight (*prajñā*). When the mind of lust, the mind of anger, and the mind of delusion are all extinguished, these three minds become purified; for one who desires to attain the path to transcend the world, it will not be difficult.”

Having attained the path of Arhatship, all lust, anger, and delusion have been extinguished; one should declare for oneself that these three matters have been abandoned, and that one will no longer engage in the phenomena of birth and death.
The Buddha called to Ānanda from Mount Suvarṇakūṭa:
"Let us proceed once more to Mount Hastadattaka.
Ānanda said:
"So be it," he replied.
He then set out together with the bhikṣus and arrived at the village of Hastigrāma.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"The mind of purity, the mind of thought, and the mind of wisdom: for one who possesses a pure mind and intention, the mind arises, and the mind of wisdom arises; as the mind of wisdom arises, there is awakening and understanding. One does not think of lust, one does not think of anger, and one is no longer deluded; thus the mind attains awakening and understanding."
The bhikṣu declared of himself:
"I have attained everything I sought, through the vision of the path of arhatship.
From the Hand-Gathering (Hastaka-āgrapura), the Buddha called out to Ānanda:
"Go to the village of Yamapūra.
Ānanda replied, "Yes."
He then went together with the bhikṣus to the village of Yamunā. The Buddha addressed the community of bhikṣus:

"The method for purifying the mind consists of the mind of reflection and the mind of wisdom. Upon reaching a state free from lust and anger, one attains the path of purifying the mind. Through the mind of reflection and the mind of wisdom, the path of generating the mind of reflection arises; through the mind of purity and the mind of wisdom, the path of opening and understanding the mind of wisdom is revealed; and through the purity of the mind of reflection, clarity is attained."
When a person has cloth that is either folded or dyed, if the cloth is clean and pure, the dye will take well;

this is because the cloth is pure. A bhikṣu possesses these three minds: the pure mind, the volitional mind, and the wisdom mind. The pure mind constitutes *śīla* (precept); the volitional mind constitutes *samādhi* (concentration); and the wisdom mind constitutes *prajñā* (wisdom).
The great mind of *śīla* consists of being without lust, without anger, and without greed.
*Samādhi* is the gathering of the mind so that it does not wander.
The destruction of arrogance means having no craving or desire in the mind and upholding the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha.
It is like a person who has a folded cloth; if the cloth is soiled and the person wishes to dye it, the color will not be bright when it is placed in the dye.

Likewise, if a bhikṣu is not settled in a mind of purity, a mind of reflection, and a mind of wisdom, it is difficult for him to attain the Path because his mind is not liberated through sitting in meditation.

The bhikṣu’s mind attained spontaneous liberation; as he sat in contemplation, he immediately beheld the heavens and fully knew the thoughts in the minds of others. He also saw the destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals according to their good and evil deeds, just as sand, stones, blue, yellow, white, and black objects beneath clear water are all made manifest because the water is pure.
One who seeks the path to transcend the world must likewise purify the mind in this way.
For example, if a mountain stream is turbid, one cannot see the sand and stones at the bottom, nor can one know its depth;
likewise, if a bhikṣu’s mind is impure, he cannot attain the path that transcends the world, because his mind is turbid.
The Buddha, departing from the village of Yamapūra, called to Ānanda:
"Let us go together to the village of Priyāla.
Ānanda replied:
"So be it. He then departed with the bhikṣus and arrived at the village of Priyaṅgu.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is a mind of purity, a mind of reflection, and a mind of wisdom—those things taught by the Teacher—the disciple should train in them. The Teacher's thoughts cannot enter the disciple's heart; rather, the disciple must straighten their own mind. A bhikṣu should purify his own mind and rectify this mind. When the mind is rectified, one attains the path that transcends the world. One should declare for oneself that the path transcending the world has been attained, thereby severing the root of birth and death."
The Buddha called to Ānanda,
"Go to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Ānanda replied:
"So be it. He then departed with the bhikṣus and arrived at the town of Pāṭaligrāma.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“The mind has three defilements: the defilement of lust, the defilement of anger, and the defilement of delusion. By maintaining a pure mind one repels the defilement of lust; by maintaining a mind of reflection one repels the defilement of anger; by maintaining a mind of wisdom one repels the defilement of delusion. A bhikṣu may truly say of himself that he has attained the path to transcend the world, severing this root of birth and death, weeping, sorrow, and anxiety.”
The Buddha again departed from the city of Pāṭaliputra and called Ānanda:
"Let us go together to the city of Vārāṇasī.
Ānanda said:
"So be it," he replied.
He then went together with the bhikṣus to sit beneath a tree to the north of the city of Venuvana.
Ānanda sat beneath a tree by his side, engaging in profound reflection and internal contemplation, when the earth shook violently.
Ānanda rose and went to where the Buddha was, and said to the Buddha:
"Why does the earth tremble so greatly?
The Buddha said:
“There are four causes and conditions for the earthquake:

First, as for the shaking, the earth rests upon the water, and the water rests upon the wind; when the wind below moves, it stirs the water, and the stirring water shakes the earth. Because the earth is thus moved, this is called the first shaking.”
If there is an Arhat who wishes to test his own path, he presses the earth with two fingers of his hand and the earth shakes; this is the second shaking.
Among them, there are devas of great majestic power who, desiring to shake the earth, cause it to shake immediately; this is the third shaking.
"The Buddha will soon enter parinirvāṇa, and the earth shall again shake violently; this constitutes the fourth shaking.
Ānanda said, "The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is indeed such that when the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, the earth shakes greatly."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is sublime and most venerable; his enlightened transformation is immeasurable. Would you like to know of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power?
Ānanda replied:
"I wish to hear and know.
The Buddha said:

"I travel throughout all the world, and whenever I arrive in a commandery or kingdom, the people who know of me come to where the Buddha is. The Buddha’s body transforms itself, adopting the dress and language of that particular country or town. I observe what kind of practices those people perform and what sūtras and precepts they know."
The Buddha then further increased his mastery of the sutras and precepts.
The people did not know who he was, nor did they know that he had come from the heavens or emerged from the earth; yet the people revered him with great respect.
I manifested myself and went to the places of all the kings; the kings asked me, "Who are you?
and I replied:
"The practitioner in this kingdom," the king asked me,
"what sutra do you practice?"
I said: "Regarding whatever sūtra you wish to ask about, I shall answer all that you inquire after.
Whatever the king found pleasing, I explained to him in full detail.
I immediately vanished through transformation, so that the king could not see me; from then on, no one knew who I was.
I arrived at the land of the Śramaṇas, where I likewise transformed myself into the appearance and speech of a śramaṇa, and I asked:
"What sūtras and precepts do you practice?"
"I know the hearts of you all, and I know your words.
Having cited the scriptures and given you my exhortations, I shall now vanish through transformation.
Then, all of you followed after me with thoughts of me, speaking thus among yourselves:
"Who is this person? Is he a deva or a ghost?
My disciples all did not know who I was, nor did I declare that I was a Buddha.

Having traveled throughout the world and completed my teaching of the Way and the scriptures everywhere, I ascended to the first heaven, the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings. Adopting the dress and speech of those heavens, I asked the devas:
"What kind of scriptures do you compose?"
The deva said, "I do not know the sūtras.
I then expounded the sūtra for him until it was finished, and immediately vanished through transformation; the deva did not even know who I was.
I further ascended to the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where I manifested the dress and speech of the Trāyastriṃśa devas. I asked the Trāyastriṃśa devas:
"What sūtras do you recite?"
The Trāyastriṃśa gods replied, "We do not know the sūtra.
After I had finished preaching the sūtra for them, I transformed and vanished; the gods did not even know who I was.
I further ascended to the third Salt Heaven (*Saindhava-deva*), where I manifested the appearance, clothing, and speech of a deity of the Salt Heaven, and I asked the Salt Heaven deities:
"What sutras do you recite?"
The deva said,
"I do not know the sūtras.
I then expounded the sūtras for him.
I further ascended to the fourth heaven above, Tuṣita, where I transformed myself into the appearance and speech of that heavenly realm and asked the devas:
"What sūtra are you practicing?"
That deity said,
"Maitreya has preached the sūtra for me.
I then preached the sūtra once more for him.
I further ascended to the fifth heaven, the Heaven of No-Contention (Avṛha), and assuming the dress and speech of that heavenly realm, I asked the devas:
"Do you know the sūtras?"
The deva said, "I do not know the sutras.
I then preached the sutras to him; having transformed and vanished, none of the devas knew who I was.
I further ascended to the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Making Use of Transformations at Will (*Nirmāṇarati*), where I adopted the dress and speech of that heaven and asked the devas:
"What sūtras do you practice?"
The deity said,
"I do not know the sutras.
I then expounded the sutra for him, whereupon he immediately vanished through transformation.
From the sixth heaven upward, none knew who I was, nor did I speak of being a Buddha.

I further ascended to the Brahma Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Vṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, and the Sudarśana Heaven. All the devas came to behold me, and I questioned them all:
"Do you know the sūtras?"

Among them, there were those who knew the sutras and those who did not; for all of them, I expounded the way of birth and death, and the way to sever the root of birth and death. Whatever sutras each of you sons delighted in, I expounded them all for you.

I imitated the clothing and speech of the heavens above; as for the other four heavens, none of their inhabitants were able to speak. When I wished to ascend, those gods could not respond to me. The twenty-fifth is named the Heaven of Emptiness-Wisdom (*ākāśa-prajñā*);

the twenty-sixth heaven is named the Entrance of Consciousness-Wisdom (*vijñāna-prajñā-praveśa*); the twenty-seventh heaven is named the Entrance of Non-Conceptual Wisdom (*asaṃjñā-prajñā-praveśa*); and the twenty-eighth heaven is named the Entrance of Non-Thought (*asaṃkalpa-praveśa*).
The Buddha said:
"There is nothing I do not see; only Nirvana is the supreme bliss.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power can not only shake the earth, but all twenty-eight heavens tremble greatly; this is brought about by the Buddha’s upright mind alone. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, Ānanda shall receive from the Buddha’s own mouth the sūtras, precepts, and the teachings of the Master."
Ānanda, you should say on the road:
"I have heard this Dharma from the Buddha’s own mouth; I shall now explain it for the sake of the future community of bhikṣus. Ānanda!
If one cannot conceal the Buddhist scriptures, they should be displayed openly; there is nothing to be doubted within the sūtras. After my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus shall together uphold the Dharma.
