If there be another bhikṣu who falsely desires to act as a teacher of the Dharma, he should discard those sūtras that lack the prohibitions and precepts, lest he uphold what ruins the Buddha-Dharma.
If there be another bhikṣu who falsely adds to or subtracts from the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha, Ānanda, you should say to him:
"I have not heard this sūtra-dharma from the Buddha; why do you falsely add to or subtract from the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha?"
"Monks, those who do not understand the Buddha’s discourses should inquire of the elder monks.

Ānanda, regarding the discourses and precepts you have seen, and that which you have heard directly from the Buddha’s own mouth, explain them to the community of monks without adding or subtracting anything."
Ānanda! If there are those who wish to increase or diminish the sūtras and the precepts, they should be placed in their proper context;
that which is not in accordance with the Dharma should be discarded and not employed. Ānanda!
If one should say,
"The Buddha did not utter these words," one should be told:

"If anyone wishes to subvert the Buddha's sutras and precepts, those among them who are deluded bhikṣus and do not understand the sutras and precepts should question the elder bhikṣus; the bhikṣus must not become angry."

If there is a bhikṣu who does not understand this sūtra, and among them there is another bhikṣu who knows the sūtras and the precepts and understands what the Buddha has taught, he should go to consult him.
If there is a bhikṣu who has doubts regarding the sūtras and the precepts, he should come and question the community of bhikṣus, who should say:
"I heard it from my teacher."
Each shall state the name of their own teacher.

When a bhikṣu recites the sūtras and precepts, he must not harbor doubts by saying, "This is not that which was commanded as a precept by the Buddha. All bhikṣus and the Saṃgha are contained within the compiled scriptures (*saṃgīta-piṭaka*). That which is within them should be used; that which is outside the compiled scriptures should be discarded and not used.

Those who have doubts and do not understand the sutras and precepts should inquire as to where there are elder bhikṣus who are learned in the sutras and precepts; they should go there to ask about those scriptures, and the questioner must not say that they are incorrect.
Should there be any who have doubts, Ānanda shall explain them orally, saying:
"I heard this from the Buddha, yet it has not been included within the compiled sūtras; since it was not spoken by the elder bhikṣus, discard it and do not use it."
"O bhikṣus, you should abide by the sūtras and the precepts; once you have taken your stand upon the sūtras and the precepts, you should uphold them together.
If there be any bhikṣu who, harboring doubts, says that this is not the true Buddha-sūtra, or who takes no pleasure in the sūtras, the bhikṣus should expel him."
When weeds grow among the grain in the world, those weeds ruin the grain’s fruit; people must weed them out and remove them, so that the grain may produce fine fruit.
Likewise, when there are evil bhikṣus who take no pleasure in the sūtras nor observe the precepts, they ruin and destroy good bhikṣus; all the bhikṣus should join together to expel them.
Among them was a virtuous bhikṣu who cherished the sūtras and the precepts; he went to where another bhikṣu was and said:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'Whatever you hold, whatever you know, and whatever you have studied, you should transmit those sūtras and precepts to other bhikṣus.'"

One should say: "When the Buddha was in the world, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a district, such-and-such a village, and at such-and-such a place, he was accompanied by such-and-such a bhikṣu and taught such-and-such a sūtra and precept. Holding to these sūtras and precepts, one must not criticize them by saying they are not the Buddha's word.
What has been spoken should be transmitted to one another for instruction and successively adopted and practiced; the elderly and the young should mutually supervise and support one another.

Do not, on account of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, fail to adopt and practice [these teachings]. When successive generations adopt and practice them, the devas and humans will all rejoice in assistance and obtain merit, thereby ensuring that the Buddha’s sūtras endure for a long time.
"After I have entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda, you should say:

'In such-and-such a place there is a bhikṣu who is learned in the sūtras and maintains the precepts; there is also a newly ordained bhikṣu. You, newly ordained bhikṣu, should go to where that elder bhikṣu learned in the sūtras resides, and from him you should receive the sūtras and the precepts.'"
When newly arrived bhikṣus hear the sūtras and precepts, they must not say that they do not uphold them; rather, they should receive and practice them together.

When bhikṣus harmoniously uphold the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts, laymen and laywomen outside the community who hear that the saṅgha of bhikṣus harmoniously upholds the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts will all joyfully provide offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for the sick to the saṅgha of bhikṣus, so that the Buddha’s sūtras may endure for a long time.

When the community of bhikṣus maintains harmony and serves one another, with those above and below mutually restraining and supporting each other, people in the world proceed toward [the higher realms].
Those who go to the paths of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts do so solely because they fail to maintain harmony with one another; thus they proceed to these three miserable destinies.

The bhikṣus who uphold the sūtras and the precepts should harmonize with one another; they must not disparage each other by saying, "I possess much wisdom" or "Your wisdom is meager. Whether one possesses much wisdom or little wisdom, each should practice according to their own way.
If the bhikṣus maintain harmony, the Buddha’s sūtras will endure for a long time; all people in the world will obtain blessings, and the devas in the heavens will all rejoice.
That which is not contained within the sūtras and the precepts should be discarded;
that which is within the Buddha’s words, as spoken by the Buddha and received by the bhikṣus, should be reverently practiced.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Proceed once more to the kingdom of Pāpīyan.
Ānanda said:
"So be it. The Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus, traveled from the kingdom of Fuyan to the kingdom of Pāpīyas, and stayed in the kingdom of Cāndana.

The people of the kingdom of Pāpīyas were called Zhuhua; when the people of Zhuhua heard that the Buddha had arrived and was staying in the kingdom of Cāndana, they all came out, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and withdrew to sit at one side. The Buddha then preached the sūtras to them all.
At that time, there was a man named Chun; Chun’s father’s courtesy name was Huashi.
While Huashi’s son was present among those seated, all the other people departed, and Chun alone remained.
After a short while, he rose, circumambulated the Buddha three times, withdrew to stand with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
"May you, together with the community of bhikṣus, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow."

The Buddha remained silent and did not respond. Chun then stepped forward, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed for his home, where he prepared seats and lit lamps for the Buddha and the bhikṣus.
The next day, Cunda came and informed the Buddha,
saying, "It is prepared.
The Buddha rose, took his bowl, and together with the bhikṣus, went to Cunda’s house for a meal.
Among the bhikṣus was a wicked bhikṣu who took a drinking vessel and broke it. The Buddha knew of this immediately, and Cunda also saw it.
When the Buddha had finished his meal, Cunda took a small stool and sat before the Buddha, addressing him:
"I wish to ask about one matter. In the heavens above and the world below, there is no wisdom that surpasses the Buddha's. How many kinds of bhikṣus are there in the world?"
The Buddha said:
"There are four classes:

first, those who are preeminent in the Way; second, those who understand the Way and are able to speak of it; third, those who live their lives in reliance upon the Way; and fourth, those who defile the Way."
What is meant by the excellence of the Path?

The meaning of the Path as it is taught is immeasurable; one who is able to practice the Great Path is most supreme and peerless. One who subdues the mind’s attitudes of sorrow and fear, acting as a guide for the world through the Dharma—such a person is a śramaṇa, and this constitutes the excellence of the Path.
What is meant by "understanding the Way and being able to speak"?

It refers to those who uphold the foremost teaching esteemed by the Buddha, who practice it without doubt or difficulty, and who are also able to expound the phrases of the Dharma for others—such as these śramaṇas are "those who understand the Way and are able to speak."
What is meant by living in accordance with the Dharma?

It is to maintain mindfulness in self-restraint, to diligently apply oneself to one's studies, to remain single-mindedly without turning back, and to persevere without weariness; when one covers oneself with both human conduct and the Dharma, such a person is a śramaṇa who lives in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by defiling the Way?
It refers to those who do only what they please, relying on their noble lineage and exclusively engaging in turbid conduct, thereby provoking debate;
they do not recollect the Buddha’s words nor do they fear the retribution of sin—such as these śramaṇas are those who defile the Way.
Ordinary people among men believe that disciples exist within the realm of purity and knowledge; some are good and some are evil, and thus they cannot all be regarded as identical.

Those who are unwholesome bring slander and defamation upon the wholesome; it is like weeds among grain, where the weeds ruin the grain’s fruit. When there is an evil son in a household throughout the world, that one son ruins the family; likewise, when one bhikṣu is evil, he ruins the other bhikṣus as well, causing all the bhikṣus to be regarded as evil.
The Buddha said:
"A person does not become beautiful by means of countenance or clothing; one whose mind is pure and upright is truly beautiful. One must not judge others by outward appearances."
The Buddha told Chun:
"If you provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, after death you shall be reborn in the heavens.

One who understands the sutras should eliminate lustful thoughts, eliminate angry thoughts, and eliminate deluded thoughts; one must not, on account of a single individual, condemn the entire assembly."

The Buddha left Cunda’s house and called Ānanda: “Go to the country of Kauśāmbī.
Ānanda replied, “Yes.”
He then set out with the community of bhikṣus from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra toward the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
On the way, the Buddha fell ill; he left the path to sit down and called for Ānanda.
Ānanda said, "Yes. The Buddha said:
"There is a stream nearby called Kukkutapada; go fetch water from it in your bowl and bring it back full, for I wish to drink and wash my face.

Ānanda immediately went there to the edge of the stream. At that time, five hundred chariots were crossing the river upstream, making the water very turbid. Ānanda took some of this turbid water and brought it back to inform the Buddha:
"There are five hundred chariots upstream on the river; the water has been greatly fouled by their passage. It may only be used for washing the face and feet, but it is not fit for drinking."
"Between here and there is another stream called the Hiraṇyavatī; its water is clear and abundant, and it is not far from here—you may go there to fetch some to drink.
The Buddha then took the turbid water and washed his face and feet, whereupon his illness was slightly alleviated.

At that time, there was a high minister from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra named Pauṇika, who was traveling along the road. From afar, he beheld the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; his appearance was upright and serene as he sat in quietude.
The minister Pāyāsi approached the Buddha, paid homage to him, and withdrew to sit at one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and Pāyāsi shed tears.
The Buddha asked:
"Which bhikṣu was preaching the Dharma to you?"
"If you have heard the sutra, for what reason do you weep?
Pāpīyān replied, "There was a man named Roca-yen who recited the sutra for me; at that time, tears fell from my eyes."
The Buddha asked,
"What sūtra are you reciting for me?
Pāyāsi replied:
“Roga was sitting beneath a tree, contemplating his own body, when five hundred chariots passed by. Not long after, a man asked him:
‘Just now five hundred chariots passed by; did you hear the sound of the chariots?’”
He replied, "I did not hear it. The man said:
“It is right here, making such a noise; why do you not hear it?
He replied, “Suddenly I did not hear it.”
The man asked,
"Was the bhikṣu asleep at that time?
He replied:
"I am not asleep.
The person asked,
"Why do you not hear the sound of the carriage?"
He replied, "I am contemplating the Way; I am reflecting upon the five internal organs of my own body.
The person said:
"The carriage passed by like this, yet I did not hear the sound of the carriage. Pāyāsi said:

"On the road, I encountered a man who preached the Sūtra to me. This bhikṣu, Rogañjaya, possessed such profound realization of the Path that he did not hear the sound of five hundred carriages; for this reason, I wept."
The Buddha asked Pāṭaliputra,
"How does the sound of five hundred chariots compare to the sound of thunder?
Pāṭaliputra replied:
"Even the sound of a thousand chariots is not equal to the sound of thunder.
The Buddha told Pāṭali:
"In the past, when I was at the Udumbara village, I sat in meditation contemplating the root of birth and death throughout the world."
At that time, a heavy rain fell with thunder and lightning strikes, killing four oxen and two brothers who were plowing.
Then, a great multitude of people went to witness the scene.
A certain person came to where I was, prostrated before me, and I asked him:
"Why have people gathered here?
The man replied:
"Only a moment ago there was a thunderclap that killed four oxen and two brothers; why did the Buddha not hear it?
Was the Buddha asleep at the time?
The Buddha replied:
"I am not asleep; I am sitting and contemplating the Way," he replied.
The man said, "The Buddha-way is thus profound that one does not hear the sound of thunder while sleeping; the Buddha’s contemplation of the Way is exceedingly deep."
The man also immediately shed tears.
The minister Pāyāsi said:
"The Way of the Buddha is thus profound; from this day forward, I shall uphold the sutras and precepts of the Buddha."
Pāyāsi immediately called his attendants and sent them back to fetch a piece of gold-woven cotton cloth, saying, "I shall offer this to the Buddha.
The attendants then returned and brought it.
Pāṭaliputra took it up and presented it to the Buddha, saying to the Buddha:
"I know that the Buddha does not need it, but please have compassion for me and accept it.
The Buddha then accepted it, and Pāṭaliputra paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha called Ānanda:
"Bring me a fine gold-woven cotton cloth; it must be of a beautiful, pure yellow color.
Ānanda replied:
"I have attended upon the Buddha for more than twenty years, yet I have never seen cotton cloth as excellent as this.
The Buddha said,
"It is indeed very excellent."
Ānanda said,
“The color of the Buddha’s face today is like the color of this cotton cloth.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The Buddha possesses such a complexion on two occasions: when the Buddha first attains the Way and becomes a Buddha, his facial complexion is thus; and tonight at midnight, when I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, my facial complexion shall likewise be thus.”
The Buddha again called to Ānanda:
"Go to the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River; I wish to bathe my body.
Ānanda replied:
"So be it. The Buddha went alone with Ānanda to the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River; there the Buddha removed his robe, took water himself, and bathed.
The Buddha then said to Ānanda:
“Early this morning, the son of the Huashi clan, Chun, fed me a meal; today at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. If you were to tell Chun:
‘After the Buddha has accepted your meal, he will enter parinirvāṇa at midnight,’ you would surely cause him great joy.”
He said to Chun: "Do not weep.

If one feeds a Buddha even once, one obtains five blessings. If you feed the Buddha, the Buddha will take the strength from your meal and enter parinirvāṇa; you, Chun, shall obtain long life, physical beauty, wealth, nobility, and birth in the heavens."
“The Buddha is worthy of veneration; by offering a single meal to the Buddha, one obtains five blessings.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“There is a bhikṣu named Candana Bhikṣu who is quick-tempered and fond of reviling others; he frequently quarrels with the other bhikṣus. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should we bhikṣus together conduct ourselves regarding the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, you all must no longer speak with him. Since the bhikṣus do not speak with him, the bhikṣu Candana should reflect upon it and harbor deep shame and remorse for having repeatedly quarreled with the bhikṣus."
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Prepare a bed with the head pointing north; my back aches greatly and I wish to lie down.

Ānanda immediately prepared the bed and placed a pillow. The Buddha lay down on his right side, with his knees drawn up and his feet stacked one upon the other, reclining to contemplate the Way of Non-action (wuwei).
As the Buddha lay down, he called out to Ānanda:
"Do you know the matter of the seven points? What are these seven?"

First, having aspiration; second, clarifying the scriptures; third, not being indolent regarding the scriptures; fourth, not being greedy for sleep but delighting in the scriptures; fifth, rectifying the mind; sixth, purifying the mind; seventh, contemplating the impurities within the body.
"A bhikṣu who possesses these seven qualities knows for himself that he has attained the path to transcend the world.
Ānanda thought to himself that the Buddha was lying down in weariness, so the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Is it because you think I am weary that you lie down?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a person is not indolent regarding the sūtras and is not indolent in their sitting and rising, desiring to become a Buddha, they may attain Buddhahood. Having finished speaking, he immediately rose from his seat.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Kapphiṇa who came and said to Ānanda,
"I wish to ask about one matter. Ānanda said:
"The Buddha’s holy body is unwell; do not [disturb him].
The Buddha immediately knew from within that the bhikṣu wished to ask a question, and he said to Ānanda:
"Call the bhikṣu to enter."
He entered and met with the Buddha, who said:
"Ask whatever you wish to ask.
The bhikṣu said:
“The Buddha has an illness; let us set aside the sutras and there is no need to speak further.
As for the seven matters spoken of by the Buddha, we have heard them and shall uphold them. Let the Buddha cease and not preach the sutras.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I was lying down just now because Ānanda, mindful of the Buddha, felt a sense of weariness and thought, 'Why is he lying down? For this reason, I arose and spoke on these seven matters."
The bhikṣu said, "The Buddha is the most honored one in the heavens above and the world below; why not request medicine from the devas so that your illness may be cured?
The Buddha said:
"Just as the houses and dwellings of people, though long-standing, must all eventually decay, while the earth remains stable as before;
so too the Buddha’s mind is as stable as the earth, while his body is like an old house. His mind is without illness; it is only his body that is ill."
The Buddha said, “One grieves over seven matters; one grieves for the body’s observance of the precepts.
The bhikṣu asked:
"Now that the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa, he even has physical illness; how much more so for ordinary people?
The bhikṣus said, "When a swallow raises its young, it relies on its parents to provide food so they may live. Now that the Buddha abandons us to enter parinirvāṇa, upon whom shall we rely?"
The World-Honored One spoke again:
“In my sutras, I have not taught that there is one who is born and yet does not die; a bhikṣu should mindfully uphold the grave precepts of the Buddha.
The bhikṣu then departed.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go quickly and prepare a bed for the Buddha at Halahala; let it be placed with the head to the north, for tonight at midnight, the Buddha shall enter parinirvāṇa."
Ānanda, having received the command, went there and arranged the bed with the head toward the north.
When he had finished, he returned and reported:
"The arrangement of the bed is complete."
The Buddha rose and went to the Yaṃgū River, where he obtained a couch and lay down on his right side.
A bhikṣu named Upavāna stood before the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Do not come before me.
Ānanda replied:
"For twenty-five years that I have personally attended him, I have never seen a bhikṣu come forward directly without first asking Ānanda.

The Buddha said, "This bhikṣu possesses the greatest majestic power among those devas; having heard that the Buddha is about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he has come straight forward out of a longing to see the Buddha."
Ānanda asked: "Is it only this deity who knows that the Buddha is about to pass into parinirvāṇa,
or are there others as well?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Within a distance of four hundred and eighty *li* from the borders of the kingdom of Kuśinagara, the deities stand shoulder to shoulder so closely that not even a needle could pass between them. All have come weeping upon hearing that the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa. Among them are those who pull out their own hair, those who tear their own clothes, and those who beat their breasts and stare vacantly at the corpse, lamenting:
'Alas! What a tragedy!'"
The Buddha has abandoned us and passed into parinirvāṇa; how swift was his departure!
The Buddha was the Great Illumination, the eye within the triple world; now that he enters parinirvāṇa, the eye of the triple world is extinguished.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "In my original scriptures, I have never said that there is no birth and no death, or that there is nothing in heaven and earth that does not decay and perish. Fools take heaven and earth to be permanent, but the Buddha regards them as empty space. Heaven and earth undergo formation and destruction; there is no one who does not cast off this body. Good and evil follow the person. If a father commits a transgression or evil, the son does not incur the calamity; if a son commits a transgression or evil, the father does not incur the calamity. Each undergoes life and death individually, and the retribution for good and evil follows each person's own body."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when we enshrine the Buddha’s body, what should be the proper procedure?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You remain silent and do not grieve; there will be renunciants and householders who shall together mourn for my body.
Ānanda said, "By what means would they mourn for the venerable body of the Buddha?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The method of burial shall be according to the funeral rites of a Cakravartin Emperor, yet the Buddha’s shall surpass even those.
Ānanda said:
“What is the method for the funeral of a Holy Cakravartin King? The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The funeral rite involves wrapping the body in fine silk cloth and then layering a thousand pieces of *karpāsa* cotton over it. This is placed within a simulated coffin, which is then doused with fragrant oils. All manner of excellent incense is applied upon it. Using firewood from the *tz'u*, *chang*, and *nan* trees, the coffin is covered; the wood is piled above and below until the cremation is complete. The *śarīra* are then collected at a crossroads, where a stūpa is erected with a *yaṣṭi* (flagpole) installed. A circular base is placed on top, silken banners are hung, and drums are suspended. Flowers, incense, and lamps are offered—such is the funeral rite for a flying emperor.”
"The Buddha is even more excellent than him.
When the Buddha spoke these words, Ānanda was behind him; overcome with emotion, he wept, resting his head against the corner of the couch, and said from behind:
"His passing is too swift; the eye of the world is lost."

The bhikṣu-saṃghas from the various districts and kingdoms in the four directions, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, came weeping and said to one another, "We fear we shall not see the Buddha again."
When the community of bhikṣus arrived,
the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Where is Ānanda?
They replied:
“Ānanda was nearby at the corner behind the couch, his head bowed, sobbing with a choked voice.
The bhikṣus shed tears and said,
“The Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One— how exceedingly swift it is!”
The Buddha said:
"When I was formerly traveling through various villages and settlements, I informed you all in advance that ninety days hence I would enter parinirvāṇa.
The disciples of the four assemblies who were thousands of li away all arrived. The Buddha then addressed Ānanda:
"Do not grieve. Why is this? For more than twenty years you have served the Buddha with all your heart;

you have been compassionate and kind toward the Buddha, reverent in body and careful in speech, and have been most filial toward the Buddha. The attendants of past Buddhas were like Ānanda, and the attendants of future Buddhas shall also be like Ānanda."
If you knew the Buddha’s intention—if you could say that at such-and-such a time the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās would be able to see him, and at such-and-such a time they would not;

if you could say whether the food and drink offered was fit to eat, fit to drink, or whether it was appropriate to rest or rise—then you would always have acted in accordance with the Buddha’s intention and never failed in propriety.
Furthermore, if you knew which bhikṣus or śrāmaṇeras delighted in the sūtras and which did not, and all your words were truthful, you would be most filial toward the Buddha. Why then do you weep?
The Buddha told them:
“Bhikṣus, listen!
The Wheel-Turning Emperor possesses four virtues that are difficult to equal.”
What are the four virtues?
All the minor kings, the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and the common people went to the imperial palace, where the Emperor of the Flying Wheel saw them all.
With a harmonious mind and gentle instruction, he spoke to the kings on the methods of governing a state: contentment and lack of craving, the conduct of a śramaṇa, and taking purity as the foremost.
The householders and the common people went out to the Buddha temples to listen to and receive the true and correct transformation of the śramaṇas; upon returning, they would practice filial piety.

According to their established needs, he bestowed gifts with a compassionate heart. Among the various kings, the Śreṣṭhis, and the common people, there were none who did not rejoice; they praised the Sage Emperor, whose influence moved the heavens.
The Emperor of Flying Spirits possesses these four virtues.
The Bhikṣu Ānanda also possesses four virtues:

whenever there are *bhikṣus*, *bhikṣuṇīs*, laymen (*upāsakas*), or laywomen (*upāsikās*) who go to Ānanda’s presence to inquire about the sūtras and the precepts, Ānanda explains them for them in full detail and at great length; none of these four classes of disciples fail to rejoice, and as they withdraw and depart, they praise him along the way—this is called Ānanda’s first set of four virtues.

Furthermore, when there are members of the four classes of disciples who do not understand the profundity of the sūtras and come to Ānanda’s presence to question him on their doubts, Ānanda unties their knots so that none remain unresolved; those who hear him never grow weary, and upon leaving, there are none who do not offer praise—this is called Ānanda’s second set of four virtues.
When the fourfold assembly of high virtue beholds Ānanda attending at the Buddha’s left side, there are none who do not praise him; this is called Ānanda’s third set of four virtues.

Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, regardless of whether the words were many or few, everything Ānanda hears he recognizes, recites, and transmits to the fourfold assembly without any addition or omission; this is Ānanda’s fourth set of four virtues.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“Not far from here there are various kingdoms—the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the kingdom of Sāketa, the kingdom of Campā, the kingdom of Rājagṛha, the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, and the kingdom of Vaiśālī. In all these great nations, the principles of the Dharma are fully understood; why does the Buddha not enter parinirvāṇa in one of them?”
"Since you are in a small district, moreover situated outside the city, will you enter parinirvāṇa in such a meager and humble place?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not say it is a small district."

Why is this so? In the distant past, in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī—formerly known as Kauśāmbavat—the realm was greatly prosperous and free from pestilence; rice and grain were abundant, the populace flourished, and every household had filial sons.

The city is four hundred and eighty li long from east to west and two hundred and eighty li wide from south to north. It has seven tiers of walls, all constructed by piling up fired brick; the city walls are adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and the walls are likewise covered with tiles made of these four treasures.
The city wall is sixty-four feet high and twenty-four feet wide at the top. Within the city are jeweled trees with flowers of five-colored radiance.
There are three roads, both sides of which are lined with the four treasures and covered with tiles.
On either side are residential dwellings, carved and inlaid with exquisite patterns; their attire is like that of the heavens, and they possess lutes, harps, and various musical instruments.

Men and women do not mingle; their songs celebrate virtue. The joy of the Way becomes ever more manifest, and the people are free from sorrow or fear. Their hearts are constantly filled with gladness; they do not adorn their heads, yet the fragrance of their clarity reaches afar.

"That holy king was named Mahāsaṃmata; he was titled a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin Emperor) who led his armies in glory throughout the world, peerless and without equal. He guided them by the Way, and none violated the royal law. When the people wished to fly, they would go wherever they thought of as soon as they conceived the thought."
The king possessed seven treasures that appeared spontaneously:

a golden flying wheel, a divinely powerful white elephant, a dark-blue divine horse, a bright moon pearl, a celestial jade maiden as his wife, a holy minister who presides over treasures, and a holy minister who commands the military.

The King possessed four virtues: during his childhood, his time as crown prince, his accession to the imperial throne, and his renunciation of the kingdom and desires to become a śramaṇa, he remained in each state for eighty-four thousand years; this was the first virtue of King Mahāsaṃmata that others could not equal.

His meals were transformed by spiritual power, his body was free from chronic illness, and his physical and mental states were always at ease due to the perfect balance of cold and warmth; these were the second two virtues.
His appearance was majestic and his countenance was peerlessly beautiful, surpassing even Śakra, whom he considered inferior; this was the third virtue.

Throughout the heavens and across the lands, from the high to the lowly, the people love their king with compassion, just as a filial son desires his parents to be at peace. The king, too, possesses a sincere heart of compassion for all beings, regarding them as his own children: he bestows wealth upon the poor, provides food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, and ensures that the destitute, the elderly, the young, and the orphaned live together as kin and children. He provides them with housing and vehicles, and swiftly cures the sick with medicine; these are called the four virtues.
"In that land, twelve kinds of sounds are constantly heard:

the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of oxen, the sound of chariots, the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of dancing, the sound of singing, the sound of various stringed instruments, the sound of reciting benevolence and righteousness, and the sound of praising the sublime conduct of the Buddha."

The clothing of the common people was woven from various jewels, interspersed with bright moons and pearls; their necklaces shone along the roads. Their food, drink, and musical performances were like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the inhabitants lived in joyful delight, with no day that they were not happy.
The King wished to go out on an excursion and summoned his charioteer, whose name was Sudatta, and commanded him, saying:
"Drive the carriage slowly; it has been a long time since I have seen the Śramaṇa Śāriputra, and I now wish to see him."

When the Śreṣṭhin Śrīman heard that the king was about to go out, those who possessed bright moon pearls, white pearls, emerald pearls, blue pearls, coral, and sandalwood incense immediately presented them as offerings to the noble king.
The King did not wish to accept them, but they all bowed their heads and entreated him with piteous pleas; only then did the King accept them.
He commanded his treasurer to double the price paid for them.
Both the common people and the great officials, both high and low, also scattered various precious flowers and incense upon the ground, invoking blessings of infinite longevity.
There were eighty-four thousand minor kings who, hearing that the Emperor of Flying Travelers intended to practice giving, all came to attend upon him and arrived at the location of the Great Hall.
The Emperor wished to ascend the main hall together with the various kings, but the kings declined, saying, "We,
your subjects, each have our own precious halls in our respective kingdoms.
The Emperor said:
"Your minor palaces are not sufficient to speak of; let us rather behold the Hall of Radiance.
Consequently, none dared to ascend.

Each of the kings possessed a precious chariot ten *zhang* in height, each with four wheels. From bottom to top, they were entirely made of the seven treasures, and atop them were hung banners and streamers whose brilliant colors shone upon one another. Each chariot was drawn by six horses, all of whom could fly through the air.
At that time, there was a carriage drawn by two white elephants, named Kurunga, which the Holy Emperor rode.
Eighty-four thousand carriages all preceded him as he proceeded to the Hall of Radiance.
"The palace was named Prabhāsa, forty *li* in length and breadth; its walls were made of bricks of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
it also had pillars made of these four treasures;
and its roof tiles were of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal."
The stairs were fifty tiers high, each made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
there were beams of gold, beams of silver, beams of lapis lazuli, and beams of crystal;
and there were crossbeams of gold, crossbeams of silver, crossbeams of lapis lazuli, and crossbeams of crystal.
Within the hall there were eighty-four thousand couches—couches of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;

canopies of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; and hangings woven of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and red wool—all spread over the couches, with pillows made of celestial fabrics woven by the gods.
“Ānanda! The palace walls are fourfold:
walls of gold, walls of silver, walls of lapis lazuli, and walls of crystal;”

He constructed four bathing pools made of the four precious substances, each measuring forty *li* in circumference. The golden pool had steps of white silver; the silver pool had steps of gold; the lapis lazuli pool had steps of crystal; and the crystal pool had steps of lapis lazuli. Within the pools, four-colored lotuses—blue, red, purple, and white—grew spontaneously, blooming constantly throughout both winter and summer. Outside the pools stood fragrant flowering trees. Beneath the terraces were four paths, with railings likewise made of the four precious substances, each railing extending twenty *li* in length.

Before the palace steps, there were four trees made of precious gems; each tree was forty li in height, and its shade covered the ground for the same distance. The golden tree had silver leaves, the silver tree had golden leaves, the lapis lazuli tree had crystal leaves, and the crystal tree had lapis lazuli leaves.

From below the hall, the Emperor reflected that it was improper for him to ascend the dais and declined the offer to do so, yielding instead to the various princes; yet none of the princes dared to ascend.

Da Kuaijian then issued an imperial decree to his attendants, requesting that those śramaṇas who had attained the state of *śaikṣa*, were clear in their mastery of the sūtras, and maintained the precepts, be invited first to the dais. He provided them with an abundance of fine food and bestowed upon them precious jewels as generous gifts.
When the śramaṇa Śreṇika had departed, the Emperor immediately reflected deeply that life is impermanent; accompanied by a single attendant, he ascended the Mingdian Hall and said:
"I wish to dismiss all my ladies and court musicians."
The attending ministers and various kings each sent him away.
The Emperor sat upon a golden throne with his feet resting on a silver footstool, and he reflected deeply:
"What benefit does this lewd conduct bring to oneself? The foolish are full of greed and do not recognize its calamity."

Although my lifespan now is three hundred and thirty-six thousand years, all that is flourishing must decline, and all that meets must part; the body is a decaying seed that will inevitably turn to ash and dust. Who, then, can long preserve these four precious palaces?
He said, "I am but a single person; a small hut is sufficient for my comfort. What need have I for a palace forty *li* in size and eighty-four thousand couches?
From the golden couches down to the silver couches, he stepped upon the golden footstools.

"Only by applying one's own mental effort can one surely purify the mind of greed, envy, anger, delusion, and sexual misconduct; by means of the four marks of impermanence, one must extinguish these so that nothing remains. Beholding the impermanence of the world, how could I possibly endure for long?"
From the silver bed he proceeded to the lapis lazuli bed, and stepping onto the crystal table, he said:

"I have eighty-four thousand jade maidens in my inner palace; I now dismiss them all, for their confinement serves no purpose. The assembly of women brings about the flourishing of evil; I must cast away these defiled thoughts."
From the lapis lazuli couch he stepped onto a crystal couch, his feet treading upon a lapis lazuli table, and reflected deeply:

"All affairs under heaven are ultimately evil; only non-action (*wuwei*) brings true joy. To rid myself of my turbid ambitions, I must seek non-action. Although I am now the Flying Emperor, possessing such great wealth and nobility, what benefit does this bring to the self?"
The attendant stepped forward and said, "The various jade maidens ask why Your Majesty remains in the palace hall for so long; they all wish to come forward.
The Emperor told the attendant:

He commanded his ministers in charge of treasures and sent forth his various consorts, each returning to her own home with the many rare and famous jewels adorning their persons, which they all took with them;
he likewise dispatched the kings, the assembly of ministers, the celestial horses, and the precious elephants, ordering them all to depart.
"King Mahāpraṇāda immediately ascended to a high terrace and heard from afar the clamor of many voices crying out to heaven. The Emperor asked:
'What sound is this?
The attendant replied:"
"The voice of a celestial jade maiden!

At these words, the kings and their ministers fell prostrate upon the ground; they raised a wail and called out to Heaven. The precious elephants and celestial horses let out mournful cries and shed tears, longing for the Heavenly King; there was none among them who did not collapse in grief.
The Emperor said,
"Bring a small stool and place it at the foot of the hall.
He then invited the Jewel of the Women, the various kings, and the assembly of officials to present the various treasures of elephants, horses, and chariots, along with their attendants.

The first legitimate consort sat by the side of the Emperor; the Emperor treated her with the affection due to a younger sister. As he attended upon the various ladies, the legitimate consort raised her hand and pointed to the various "jewel-women," saying:

"The countenances of these celestial maidens shine brilliantly upon the world; they wear heavenly robes rarely seen in this world. I pray you will lend them your slight attention to fulfill their intentions.

As for the precious elephant and the celestial horse—the horse named *Huanqing*—and the white pearls, night-shining gems, and various jeweled necklaces, their radiant splendor illuminates the kingdom."
"The kings of the four quarters all possess the wisdom of sages; they reverently serve as your subjects, being filial, compassionate, loyal, and devotedly admiring of the Heavenly King.
King Kṣemadarśin said: "For generations I have maintained a heart of compassion.

Yet among the women of this world, there is mutual jealousy; its calamities and evils spread and even reach the person of the king. Fearing this grave misfortune, I wish to distance myself from it. From this day forward, you women shall all be my sisters."
All the ladies raised their voices in lamentation, saying,
"How can you abandon us and depart while we are still alive?
They all stripped off their various ornaments and cast them upon the ground.
The principal consort tore at her hair and beat her breast, wailing in grief and crying out:
"O Heavenly King!
Upon whom shall I rely?"
The Emperor said:
"Human life is exceedingly short, yet your anxiety is protracted; the body is a decaying vessel, and death awaits without fixed date.

From this day forth, I shall hold my mind steadfastly, honoring the virtue of the śramaṇas, distancing myself from women and drawing near to the worthy and virtuous. I shall revere only the Way, cultivating my person and worrying for myself alone, unable to worry for anything else."
He addressed the kings, saying:

"Life is short while anxieties are long; you should cherish your own persons. Since there is no birth that does not end in death, you should rectify your minds and conduct, practicing compassion, love, filiality, and obedience; for glory is difficult to preserve for long."
The various kings bowed their heads and spoke with utmost sincerity:

"The nations of the four quarters all serve Your Majesty. We have often heard the holy ones praise this land, deeming it beyond compare; from the Emperor down to the ministers, none are not sagely and divine, and the treasures of the realm are like those in the heavens. May Your Majesty take pity on us and deign to return your sacred thoughts to us."
The Emperor told the kings:

"Human life has become exceedingly short, yet worldly anxieties are conversely long-lasting. You should concern yourselves with your own persons; life exists but in a breath, and there is no birth without death. You must abandon the conduct of greed, lust, and defilement."

The Emperor rose and ascended the hall, where he sat upon a golden throne. Maintaining a heart of vast compassion, he turned toward his consorts, the various ministers and kings, the common people, the elephants and horses, and all those suffering throughout the ten directions; moved by a heart of pity, he wished for them to know the Buddha. From the golden throne he moved to a silver throne, contemplating the Way of non-action (*wuwei*); from the silver throne he moved to a lapis lazuli throne, contemplating acts of compassionate mercy to rescue sentient beings; from the lapis lazuli throne he moved to a crystal throne, contemplating the practice of great filial piety, desiring to deliver his kin from across countless kalpas, while reflecting upon the foul secretions of his own five viscera and nine orifices.
The Emperor said:

"In the past, I suffered from a certain ailment that was like a bamboo rope strangling my neck and a wooden chisel boring into my body. Since the body is but a vessel of suffering, how can it be relied upon?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The Universal Monarch Mahāsudarśana was none other than myself.
After the King’s life ended, he ascended to be born in the Brahma Heaven. Who would have known that the Buddha’s body had once been a Universal Monarch who practiced the True Dharma?”

Furthermore, there are four virtues: the seven treasures appear spontaneously, extending four hundred and eighty *li* in length and two hundred and eighty *li* in width from the borders of Kauśāmbī, all situated within the city. Previously, I used the sevenfold mindfulness to place my body within this ground; now that I have attained the cessation of seeking, I contemplate the concentration of emptiness and signlessness, severing the source of birth and death. From this day forward, I shall no longer take on a physical form.
“Ānanda! Go into the city and announce to the people:
‘At midnight tonight, the Buddha shall enter parinirvāṇa. Whatever doubts you may have, go quickly to resolve them; be careful not to regret it later by harboring long-lasting, dim resentment.’”
The Buddha was staying in a small village, having departed from where he had received his precepts. Ānanda followed his instructions, and the people all said in unison:
"For what reason does the Buddha dwell in this small village and then pass into parinirvāṇa?"

The people all threw themselves to the ground; some struck their heads against the earth, some slapped their cheeks, some beat their breasts and scratched their faces, and others tore their clothes and trampled the ground while wailing and crying out, "Alas! What shall we do!"
When the king heard this, he was startled and asked,
"What sorrow is this?
The king dispatched a close minister to inquire what sorrow lay outside.
The people said with choked voices, "Ānanda commanded us, saying:
'The Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; whatever doubts or knots remain in your minds, you must come to him to resolve them.'"
"It is because of this that they are so sorrowful.
The minister returned and reported:
"Ānanda has instructed the people that the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; he told them to clarify whatever doubts they may have, and for that reason they are weeping."
The King immediately summoned his crown prince, Achen, and commanded him, saying:

"Go to the place where the Buddha is, bow your head at the Buddha's feet, and respectfully inquire after his well-being, saying: 'I humbly pray that the World-Honored One will ascend the path of Nirvāṇa within this great capital city, and not enter Parinirvāṇa in a small village.'"
The Prince said,
"If the World-Honored One does not indeed fly away like this, what shall we do?
The King replied:
"Receive these instructions and return quickly.
When the Prince arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, Ānanda said to him:
"The King of Kauśāmbī has sent the Prince here; I did not dare to announce his arrival."
The Buddha said,
"Call Ānanda.
The Prince prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew to kneel upright, assenting.

"The King has sent Āccha to bow his head at the Buddha’s feet and respectfully inquire after your well-being. Sentient beings are submerged in a deep abyss, and only the Buddha can rescue them; yet now you are about to enter parinirvāṇa—how exceedingly swift! Why should this occur within a small village rather than within the palace?"
The Buddha told Aciravata:
"Inform your father the king that I have already spoken of this: in the past, I was the Universal Monarch, the final holy sovereign, named Mahāsudarśana."
"I have already lost my body here seven times, making this the eighth.
Now that I have perfected the Way, I shall no longer let my body be cast into this earth.
I bid farewell to your father, the King, for having caused such grievous suffering to the Prince."
The Crown Prince returned to the palace, and just as darkness fell, he went to see the King and recounted the matter from beginning to end.
The King was struck with amazement and shed tears; he then issued a decree to the common people of the realm, commanding that all within the land go forth to receive the Buddha’s clear Dharma.
When the hour of midnight had arrived, the king went to the Buddha's location together with a multitude of one hundred and forty thousand people, remaining outside.
The king said to Ānanda:
"I and these one hundred and forty thousand people wish to receive the Buddha’s precepts."
Ānanda turned toward the Buddha and related the King’s intention in full. The World-Honored One immediately said, "It is suffering for both the king and the people.
Ānanda addressed him, saying:
"Would it be permissible to dismiss the King?
The Buddha said, "It is not."
"I shall meet with you.
The king, together with the men of high virtue and wisdom in the kingdom, advanced; they all prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha's feet, then withdrew to stand with palms joined.
At that time, there was no lamp or fire before the Buddha; the Buddha emitted light from the crown of his head, and the light shone for two thousand li.
The Buddha thanked the king, his ministers, and the people for their trouble in coming so far.
The king bowed his head and said,
"What admonitions does the Buddha have that I should practice and uphold?
The Buddha said:
"I told the messenger: 'I have received the Buddha’s discourse on the sutras for forty-nine years; the worthy ones of the kingdom shall all practice them themselves.
Your Majesty, please return to the palace; tonight at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"
The king, his ministers, and the common people all raised their voices in lamentation.
The Buddha said to the king, "I have heard that wherever there is birth, there is no lack of decay and death; why do you weep?"

Subdue the mind of fury; emulate the celestial palace above; distance yourself from evil and cherish yourself; cultivate virtue with diligence and draw near to the worthy. When affairs arise, reflect deeply; do not act with sudden violence. Human life is difficult to obtain; you ought to have compassion for the myriad people.
Those who are wise may be held accountable, while the foolish should be pardoned. The world abounds in various evils; therefore, cherish yourself and rejoice in your own well-being.
The king and the worthy one both withdrew; the king went five *li* from the Buddha and halted there.
In the city was an elder named Subhadra, one hundred and twenty years of age, who was at that time within the city.

Awakening from sleep at night, he saw the Buddha’s radiance illuminating the entire city; finding not a single person in his house, he immediately left the city and hurried to the Buddha’s location, where he said to Ānanda:
"Please allow me to report this: I have doubts regarding the World-Honored One."
Ānanda said, "It is already past midnight; the Buddha is about to pass into parinirvāṇa, so do not cause him further disturbance.
Subhadra replied:
"I cannot believe this! I have heard that only once in countless eons does a Buddha appear. Now I have come to resolve my doubts, yet you do not grant me an audience.
My doubts can only be dispelled by a Buddha; no one else is capable of doing so."
Ānanda said:
"Stop! There is no need to ask."
The Buddha, knowing that Subhadra was outside wishing to inquire about his doubts, called Ānanda and asked:
"Why did you not inform me of Subhadra’s doubts?
Ānanda replied:

Seeing that it was already midnight and that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, they feared that his arrival would cause disturbance through their talk; for the Buddha was now about to abandon the three realms of existence and the realm of desire to proceed toward the path of the unconditioned.
The Buddha said, "Bring Subhadra in; if he has any doubts, he should ask.
Ānanda then led Subhadra inside.
Upon hearing that he was about to enter, Subhadra’s heart leaped with joy and his entire body trembled; he then prostrated himself before the Buddha’s feet with his head touching the ground.
Seeing that Subhadra was elderly and his breath was faint, the Buddha granted him a stool so that he might sit.
The Buddha asked Subhadra,
"What doubts do you have? He replied:

“The Buddha is the God among Gods of the three realms; his divine sanctity is immeasurable and his supreme honor is peerless. For forty-nine years he has opened the way for transformation and guidance, such that neither immortals nor sages, nor Brahmā or Śakra, have failed to bow their heads in reverence. I have eight like-minded companions—Guishi, Wuxianshi, Zhihangshi, Bailuzi, Yanshou, Jijinfan, Duojijuan, and Nigianzi. Yet the wisdom of these eight men lacks even the light of a firefly or a candle; their goodness does not provide even a hair’s breadth of nourishment. Within they harbor the three poisons, and without they run after desires; they sit and compose empty discourses and recklessly write down what is not true. Is it possible that they will come to receive his transformative teachings?”
The Buddha told Subhadra:
"The intent of your scriptures contradicts that of the Buddha's scriptures; do they serve as a path to birth and death, seeking wealth and status?
The aim of my Way is to sever all seeking and contemplate emptiness; it does not desire worldly glory, but finds joy in detachment and non-action."
Subhadra asked,
"What is called the Way of the Unconditioned?
The Buddha said:
"To extinguish existence and return to the source, no longer undergoing birth and death—this is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for your inclinations, they are all characterized by the eight evils.
What are these eight?"
To sacrifice to ghosts and spirits and engage in vain divinations and slaughtering—this is the first.
To live as a householder with gluttonous greed, failing to uphold the way of filial piety, coveting myriad evils, and desiring without restraint or cessation—this is the second.
Divisive speech, harsh abuse, false speech, and frivolous chatter—never presenting what is good to cause the ignorant to abandon evil; these constitute three.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lewdness; these constitute four.

Constantly harboring anger, being unfilial toward one's parents, treating siblings, wife, children, and the nine branches of the clan with contempt, having a depraved mind and impure conduct, failing to encourage others toward goodness, and always being arrogant while desiring others to fear and revere him—these are the five.

To harbor depravity day and night, to fear neither law nor discipline, to treat the worthy with contempt, to honor the defiled and impure, to distance oneself from the upright and true, and to associate with evil people—this is the sixth.
Seventh: Upon hearing that there are virtuous and wise śramaṇas or brahmins who are well-versed in the scriptures, one harbors resentment and jealousy from the outset, falsely slandering them;

furthermore, one fails to revere one's ancestors or practice filial piety toward one's parents, abandons the wise and bright while instead acting as a villain, destroys benevolence and uprightness, and remains unaware of the defilement and shamefulness of worldly customs.
These are called the eight evils.
If one were to state personally:
"In the forty-nine years that the World-Honored One preached the sutras, there were eight people who did not come to receive his transformation."
"Your followers all harbor these eight evils; how could they delight in pure transformation?
Even if they were to come, the Buddha would not accept them, Subhadra!"
If your mind possesses these eight evils, you must carefully refrain from asking the Buddha:
"By observing these eight precepts, can one attain the stage of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, or Arhat?"
"Practicing these eight precepts, one must rectify the mind; only then is one a disciple of the Buddha.

If there are ordinary people who presume themselves to be teachers, guides, or leaders of instruction, yet violate these eight precepts, they are all demonic sorcerers; one should distance oneself from and avoid them, and take care not to listen to or accept their teachings."
The World-Honored One said:
"I am now alone in the three realms, walking without equal;
regarding what you doubt, ask without hesitation."
Subhadra bowed his head, knelt with his knees on the ground,
and said, "Truly, as the Buddha has spoken, I nearly lost my life and fell into madness and folly.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
“Have you understood the eight precepts?
He replied, “I have understood them.”
Bowing his head again, he said:
"I wish to cast off my lowly conduct and uphold the pure practice of a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One spoke once more:
"Is this truly so? He replied,
"I pray that the Buddha will show me compassion and accept me as a śramaṇa."

As soon as he spoke, Subhadra’s hair fell off naturally and the *kāṣāya* robe was upon his body. With a refined mind contemplating the teaching, he suddenly became free of discursive thought; his single-minded purity was like a bright moon-pearl, and he immediately attained the path of the Arhat (*arhat*).
He then reflected again: "I must not allow my teacher to enter *nirvāṇa* before me."
At that moment, the former Buddha entered the path of *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha then called to the bhikṣus, saying:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if there are people of this world who renounce their homes to cast off defilement and wish to become śramaṇas, entering among the community of bhikṣus, they must first undergo a three-month trial to test whether their practice is superior or inferior."
In the world there are four kinds of people:
the first kind are those who are so impoverished that they cannot support themselves and wish to become bhikṣus;
the second kind are those who are burdened by debts and have no means to repay them and wish to become bhikṣus.
One group, while still in their period of service, found no use for it and wished to become bhikṣus;

another group of noble persons, whose conduct was pure and untainted, heard that only once in countless ages does a Buddha appear, and upon seeing the Buddha’s scriptures, they were joyfully awakened in mind, renounced their homes and abandoned desire, and not coveting worldly glory, came to become bhikṣus.

After my parinirvāṇa, whoever comes shall be observed in their aspirations, watched in their deportment, examined in their speech, scrutinized in their gait, and known in their conduct; one shall discern where their goodness or evil tends, how they apply their mind in seeking the Way, and whether they are diligent and joyful.
After three months of examination, if his resolve is lofty and his conduct is pure, and he is approved by the assembly, he may be ordained as a bhikṣu.
Once he has become a bhikṣu, one who is senior and well-versed in the Vinaya should be selected to serve as his preceptor, who shall confer upon him the ten precepts.

Having observed the precepts for three years with constant vigilance and without deficiency, and being approved by all the virtuous ones, he shall be granted the two hundred and fifty precepts; of these, the ten precepts constitute the foundation, while the two hundred and forty precepts constitute the ritual decorum.
If you of later generations practice this Dharma, the celestial deities and terrestrial spirits will all revere and rejoice.
You bhikṣus must reflect deeply upon the precepts taught by the Buddha; do not, on the pretext that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, become indolent or violate the Dharma.

The conduct of the Buddha and the reflections of his disciples involve the young and the old honoring one another; there is no lack of filial piety here. Those who do not delight in attaining the Way or who long for noble glory should read this sutra. Those who seek longevity and desire to be reborn in the heavens should read this sutra.
The great essence of the Buddha’s teaching is to incline toward the path of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
After my parinirvāṇa, you must not say, "Because the Buddha has departed," and thus have nothing further to rely upon; you should instead rely upon the sūtras and the precepts.

After my parinirvāṇa, you shall successively transmit and uphold [the Dharma], studying the sūtras and revering the precepts; you shall observe the two hundred and fifty precepts and respectfully honor one another, just as a filial child serves its parents.
Senior bhikṣus should instruct their successors as if I were still present.
If junior bhikṣus fall ill, senior bhikṣus should attend to them with a compassionate heart, providing care and observation.
When explaining the reading of the sutras, instruct them with harmony; when they uphold the Buddha’s precepts in accordance with the Way, my teaching may endure for a long time.
After I have entered *nirvāṇa*, worthy sons and worthy daughters will, in their subsequent reflections, remember:
"In our world there was a Buddha, and there were wondrous and sublime scriptures."

"On the day the Buddha first enters parinirvāṇa in this world, you disciples shall all possess the utmost filial piety toward the Buddha and a compassionate heart for the sutras; when your lives come to an end, you shall all ascend to heaven."
"You must not, on account of my departure, fail to uphold the sutras and precepts;
be careful not to be indolent or arrogant. O Bhikṣus!
Behold the Buddha’s countenance well; the Buddha cannot rise again. Only after fifteen billion, seven hundred and sixty million years shall there be another Buddha."
A Buddha’s world is difficult to encounter; the sutras and the Dharma are difficult to hear; the Sangha is difficult to meet; indeed, it is only a Buddha who is difficult to behold.
Within Jambudvīpa there is a sovereign king of trees named Udumbara; it bears fruit but has no flowers. When the Udumbara tree bears golden blossoms, only then does a Buddha appear in the world.

"I am now about to enter parinirvāṇa. If any among you have doubts or entanglements regarding the sūtras, you should resolve those doubts while the Buddha is still present. Do not fail to release these entanglements now, lest you later dispute and wrangle; while I am here, you must urgently question me on what you doubt."

At that time, Ānanda was behind the Buddha; bowing his head, he said to the Buddha, "Since the Blessed One’s teaching and transformation, there has been no one among the community of bhikṣus who harbors doubts or fetters.
Thus did the disciple speak of himself.
“We have no doubt,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The night is already half-past; do not make any further sound.

The Buddha rose and sat upright, contemplating deeply the origin of the Way. He cast aside both good and evil throughout the triple world. Having reached the age of seventy-nine, he sought only to sever the abyss of the revolving flow of birth and death.

He contemplated with deep insight, proceeding from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; then, returning from that sphere back into his own body, he reflected upon the four elements and the impurities within his body, finding not a single thing worthy of treasure. With his head toward the north, his hand as a pillow, lying on his right side with his knees drawn up and his feet stacked one upon the other, he entered final nirvana.
Heaven and earth shook violently; the various devas scattered flowers and incense, weeping and crying out in grievance:
"The Dharma King has entered parinirvāṇa; upon whom shall we rely?
A multitude of one hundred and forty thousand kings prostrated themselves, calling out to the Buddha:
"The sentient beings are suffering great decline;
what can be done about this pain? Some even fainted and then revived.
The second Śakra addressed the devas, saying:
"The Buddha has always said that those who are born cannot avoid death; you all should contemplate the truths of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and no longer weep.
The Seventh Heavenly King also rushed down and said:
"The Buddha’s radiance has already faded; even the Buddha has abandoned his body—what hope can you have?"
"Those who weep and fall prostrate—can they ever recover?
Some bhikṣus rolled upon the ground, weeping and saying, "The Eye of the Three Realms has been extinguished; how swift was it!"
"From this day forward, the world will fall into perpetual decline.
Some wept aloud; some stood with their breath suspended, staring at the corpse; others reflected deeply:
"The Buddha was always saying:..."
"There is no birth and no death.
To weep for the body—what benefit does this bring to the clear Dharma?
A bhikṣu named Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
“Cease, O bhikṣus; do not let there be further lamentation.
Cease, O King, ministers, and people; cease, O gods above;
do not wail any longer. Ānanda asked:
"If one were to look at the various heavens above, how many people could there possibly be?

He replied, "Within a circumference of four hundred and eighty li, they are all noble devas standing shoulder-to-shoulder; if one were to drop a small needle upon them from above, the needle would not fall to the ground."
Anuruddha ascended to stop the devas, and the devas wailed with redoubled grief.
Anuruddha said to Ānanda:

"The Buddha did not command us to perform the enshrouding and interment. Go and inform the Śākyas of the passing; we shall handle the enshrouding and burial ourselves. By the World-Honored One’s decree, let the Śākyas of Kapilavastu perform the enshrouding and burial so that there may be no cause for regret."
Ānanda immediately went to the householder Śreṇika and related the matter as it had occurred.
The householder Śreṇika raised a cry of lamentation, saying:
"The World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa; we are left orphaned and exposed. The wise man is gone, and we relied solely upon the World-Honored One."
The five hundred people went to the king and petitioned him, saying:
"We beg that you allow us alone to perform the funeral rites.
The king said:

"The Buddha has departed and sentient beings are left orphaned and exposed; with a harmonious mind free from strife, one must fulfill the heart of filial piety. The Buddha takes pity on his children and causes them to obtain great blessings.
When the King spoke these words, there was no one who did not choke back tears.
The householders and the common people lifted the Buddha’s golden bed and returned toward the royal city.

The devas covered the Buddha’s bed with canopies of renowned jewels; banners and streamers led the procession, while flowers, incense, and various gems fell beneath them like snow. Twelve kinds of music were played from behind, and among the devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, there was none who did not wail in mourning.
The householder asked, "When the World-Honored One was alive, he gave instructions regarding the enshrinement and burial in a coffin;
what were those rites? Ānanda replied:
"It was said when the Buddha was in the world:
'According to the laws of a Cakravartin Emperor, the Buddha surpasses them even further.
The householder asked:
"What are the regulations for the enshrouding of a holy sovereign?
He replied:
"Use new, fine silk to firmly wrap the body, and then wrap it again with new *karpāsa* cloth."
He was placed within a provisional coffin and drenched with fragrant oils until they permeated his entire body; then the lid was placed over him.

Sandalwood, agarwood, catalpa wood, and camphor wood were piled above and below the coffin, extending thirty *zhang* in height and breadth on all four sides. Fire was set to cremate the body, while the twelve categories of music were performed simultaneously.

They scattered excellent incense and flowers over it, collected the relics while removing the ashes and charcoal, washed them thoroughly with fine fragrant liquid, and placed them inside a golden urn.

Place the urn upon a golden bed and set it within the palace, specifically in the Hall of Fasting and Purification. When ninety days have passed, one should erect a stupa and install a banner-pole at a crossroads, hanging silk streamers and offering pennants, flowers, incense, and music;
such is the funeral rite for a Wheel-Turning Emperor (Cakravartin), yet the Buddha shall surpass it.
The various *śramaṇas* and practitioners of the mind shed tears and said:
"We accept. We shall surely follow your clear instructions; we pray that you grant us seven days."
The householders addressed the king together, saying:
"We wish to enshroud the holy body of the World-Honored One; we pray that Your Majesty will attend to it.
The king said:
“With respect, we accept.

The householders together lifted the Buddha’s golden bed and returned, entering through the western gate of the city. They stayed in the center of the city for seven days, during which they gathered a multitude of three hundred thousand people who all joined in the encoffining. The populace provided twelve kinds of musical performances and lit lamps day and night; the fires extended from the city for twelve *li*, with a lamp at every step.

The second Śakra, leading a multitude of one hundred thousand devas, descended from above, bringing with him the twelve divisions of celestial music. Flowers, incense, and various jewels were suspended in the air at a distance of three li from the ground.
Śakra alone descended and asked Aniruddha,
"What instructions has the Buddha given?
Aniruddha then related the Buddha's teaching to Śakra in full detail.
The commentary says:
"I wish to perform the funeral rites with an array of precious jewels, music, flowers, incense, and burial implements;
would this be appropriate? He replied:
"I shall go to consult him.
Ānanda related the details of Śāriputra’s intention to Āniruddha, who replied:

"When the Buddha was alive, did he not issue a command to the devas and kings that no one was to perform the enshrouding and burial? He commanded that Śreṇika and the householders should handle the funeral rites."
He thanked the Brahmās and Śakras, saying, "I pray that you will clarify the Buddha's intention.
He then returned and reported Ānanda’s words in full to the devas.
The devas said:
"Are the funeral provisions for me, the Son of Heaven, not inferior to those of the common people?
He replied, "What kind of words are these?
"The World-Honored One has issued a solemn and weighty decree: 'Be careful not to criticize one another.
When the Śreṣṭhin and the householders heard this, they said, "Let us lift the couch bearing the Buddha’s relics and enter through the western city gate," but the couch would not be lifted.
The householders all said, “The bed does not move; how can he have gone out of the city?
Ānanda asked Aniruddha:
"Why does the bed not shake?
He replied,
"Because the devas wish to receive the body for enshrouding and interring, they have caused the bed not to lift."
Aniruddha said,
"I shall now ascend to inform Brahmā and Śakra and the various devas.
He immediately ascended and informed Brahmā and Śakra, saying:
Ānanda declined the intentions of the various devas regarding the funeral rites, saying, "This is the Buddha’s own intention.
The Brahmā and Śakra devas said, "We have brought these funerary implements here;
may we not be permitted to stand on the right side of the bier, while the king and the common people stand on the left, as we escort the World-Honored One with music, flowers, and incense?"
He replied, "I shall return to inform you.
Anuruddha returned and reported the celestial intention in full to Ānanda, who said:
"If one wishes to enshroud [the body] in a coffin, it would contravene the Buddha's teachings;
however, it is permissible to perform funeral rites out of filial piety.
He then informed Brahmā and Śakra accordingly.
When this matter was approved, all the devas rejoiced and descended to the right side of the Buddha’s golden couch, while the King and the populace took their places on the left side.
The householder asked,
"May the Buddha's couch be lifted and carried out through the western city gate?"

Ānanda replied, "It may be so. Śakra approached and held the front right leg of the couch with his hand; Brahmā held the rear right leg; Ānanda held the front left leg; and the king held the rear left leg. The Śaikṣas and householders bound the two front legs of the couch with silk ribbons. The devas wailed in grief as they together drew the golden couch. The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas scattered flowers, various jewels, and famous incenses, and accompanied them with music, banners, flags, and canopies. The king and the common people likewise provided such offerings.

Above, the devas and humans sang dirges in praise of his virtue; below, the common people followed with mournful songs. Devas, spirits, dragons, emperors, and commoners alike were simultaneously struck with grief; beating their breasts, they cried out that the Buddha’s passing was like this—what reliance shall sentient beings have?
Exiting through the western city gate, they proceeded toward the Pāṇḍava Hall. There was a great lecture hall, and the Buddha’s body was placed upon its dais.

Following the Buddha’s final instructions, the lay devotees wrapped his body in fine silk; then, a thousand layers of *karpāsa* cloth were wound crosswise over it. He was placed within a simulated coffin, which was then saturated with fragrant oils until they permeated the entire body. A celestial canopy was spread over it. The lay devotees together lifted the coffin down from the hall and, in the central courtyard, prepared a pyre of sandalwood, agallochum, catalpa, camphor, and cypress wood, thirty *zhang* high and wide. Devas, spirits, nāgas, kings, and the common people all scattered flowers and incense upon the funeral wood.
The householder lit the firewood, but the fire would not ignite.
He asked Aniruddha,
"For what reason does the fire not burn when I try to light it?"
He replied:

"The Buddha has an elder disciple named Mahākāśyapa, who travels everywhere to teach and transform others. He is now returning with two thousand disciples and countless devas, wishing to see the Buddha in person so that the fire shall not burn."
The householder replied,
“Yes,” and was instructed to wait.
Kāśyapa arrived together with five hundred disciples from each of the four assemblies, resting along the way.

There was a heterodox practitioner named Upatiṣya who had come from the presence of the Buddha, carrying celestial flowers called māndārava. Seeing Mahākāśyapa followed by two thousand disciples, Upatiṣya approached Mahākāśyapa, bowed his head, and completed his salutations with deference.
Kāśyapa asked,
"Where have you come from?
He replied:
"I have come from the country of Nādikā.
Kāśyapa asked,
"Do you know my Great Teacher, the Buddha?"
“I acknowledge it; I remember it.
It has been seven days since his parinirvāṇa, and it was from him that I obtained these celestial flowers.”

At that time, among the disciples, there were those who had not yet realized the Truth; upon hearing of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they were all struck with alarm and astonishment. They leaped about and beat their breasts, rolling on the ground in grief until they nearly fainted, crying out:
"Alas! What shall become of sentient beings? Who will they rely upon?"

There were those who had realized the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya) and who deeply heeded the Buddha’s admonitions: "The world is entirely impermanent; even affection is like an illusion—who can achieve eternal existence?

Among the assembly of bhikṣus, there was one bhikṣu who was elderly and dull-witted, failing to grasp the Sage’s intent. Seeing the bhikṣus in such profound and intense mourning, he stopped them and said:
"I pray you, do not grieve."

"When the World-Honored One was present, the Dharma and the precepts were so numerous and overlapping that we would say, 'This is not the Dharma' or 'That is not the meaning,' yet by maintaining this practice, we were without transgression or offense.
Now that the World-Honored One has passed away, we are free; is this not a joy?"
The assembly of bhikṣus all censured him together and consequently informed the deva; the deva seized the old bhikṣu and cast him outside the assembly. Mahākāśyapa then commanded the bhikṣus:
"Make haste to set out on the road."

The fourfold assembly of disciples and countless devas and humans, weeping as they walked, together arrived at the place where the Buddha was. They circumambulated the hall three times and prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground; they struck their faces against the earth until it was covered in dust, and some vomited blood and fainted.
Kāśyapa gazed intently at the Buddha’s golden coffin and thought to himself:
"I have come too late; I did not reach my Teacher in time, and I do not know where the World-Honored One's head and feet are located."
The Buddha, responding to the sound of his voice, extended both feet.
Kāśyapa immediately placed his head at the Buddha’s feet, extolled the Buddha’s virtues, and spoke in verse:
“He is one who is neither born nor aged, And he is one who does not die.”
He shall no longer encounter them, nor shall there be any mutual hatred upon meeting;
he shall no longer cause those he loves to be separated from one another.
One should seek the skillful means to bring about this state.
He has brought these five aggregates to an end and will not receive them again;
he no longer acts for the sake of further becoming, nor does he undergo the reception of these five aggregates.
Suffering has been completely exhausted, and its fundamental source has also been eliminated.
One should seek skillful means to attain this state.
When the Buddha has severed worldly existence and brought desire to an end,
it is called "patience," and one also abandons all worldly afflictions.
The Buddha acts for his own peace and also brings peace and security to the world;
you should simply join your palms and pay humble homage to the Buddha.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is the most luminous in the world.
The Buddha is the supreme path of vision, secure and unimpeded.
He also brings life to the world, so that beings shall no longer undergo old age and death.
What could one do for the world such that people would not receive the Buddha’s grace?
The moon rises only to dispel the darkness of night;
the sun rises only to bring light to the day;
