and lightning flashes only to illuminate the clouds.
The Buddha’s wisdom has emerged as light, illuminating the three realms.
Of all rivers, none surpasses the Kunlun River;
of all great waters, none surpasses the ocean.
Among all the luminous stars, the moon is the most brilliant;
so too, among the worlds, the Buddha is the most honored, both above and below heaven.
Because the Buddha has delivered the world, he bestows blessings that endure to this day.
The Buddha’s instructions for practice remain clear and distinct even to this day;
likewise, they remain so today for the disciples of the Buddha to receive and practice.
All gods and humans likewise pay homage with palms joined in reverence.

When Kāśyapa had finished his praise, the devas, ghosts, nāgas, kings, emperors, and common people all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Once the assembly had completed their salutations, the feet returned into the coffin.
When the devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons saw his feet sink back into the earth, they were overcome with such grief that they choked with emotion and wept together.
Having finished their lamentation, Kāśyapa and the bhikṣus offered mutual condolences to one another.
As the householder Śreṇika set fire to his dwelling, the heavens scattered flowers and incense, all crying out, "Alas, what will become of these sentient beings?
The Buddha’s light shone through to the seventh Brahma heaven;

in the hidden and dark recesses of the ten directions where beings could not see one another, they were suddenly made radiant by the Buddha’s radiance, and with joyful faces, they spoke as if in conversation: [The original Chinese text provided is incomplete at the end.]
"What light is this? the various householders asked as they deliberated.

When the Buddha’s flesh and blood had been consumed, they immediately poured fragrant milk over the fire to extinguish it. They thoroughly washed the *śarīra* (relics) and placed them in a golden urn; the Buddha’s inner and outer robes remained intact as before, while the *kārpāsa* (cotton) used to wrap his body was completely charred.

They took the reliquary urn and placed it upon a golden bed, returning to the palace where it was set down in the main hall. Gods and humans scattered flowers and performed music; lamps were lit at every step around the city walls, until the ground for twelve *li* was filled with light.
Ānanda said to Aniruddha:
"Bid farewell to the devas and nāgas, and let each of you return to your respective abodes.
The devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all shed tears and said:
“The sun and moon of the three realms have perished; the world has suffered a long-term decline. How much longer can this state of mourning last? Why do you urgently urge us to depart?”
He replied, "The populace is in great agitation, wishing to offer flowers and incense; it would be appropriate for you to return for a short while so that they may express their devotion.
Śakra then questioned Aniruddha:
"On what day shall the ancestral temple of the World-Honored One be established?
Ānanda asked Āniruddha. Ānanda replied:
" Ninety days from now, you shall establish a pillar and construct a temple at a crossroads.
The devas all said,
"If we wait ninety days, will there be a karmic affinity?"
Aniruddha said, "The disciples of the four assemblies who are far away will surely hasten here to fulfill their expectations.

Then, all the devas simultaneously prostrated themselves with their heads touching the ground; Śakra stood at the front, with the other devas as his attendants, circumambulating the hall three times before departing in mournful weeping.

Twenty thousand bhikṣus remained to guard the śarīra. He then took leave of the king and returned to his palace; together with the ministers, they prostrated themselves on the ground in grief and circumambulated the hall three times before returning to their quarters. He then commanded all the ladies and court attendants to observe the precepts for a full ninety days.

The monks and lay followers were likewise solemn and reverent; hearing from afar that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly of Kauśāmbī brought flowers and incense, their lamentations filling the roads as they circumambulated the hall three times. Prostrating themselves upon the ground, they stamped their feet in grief and cried out in anguish, "What shall we do?"

The kings within a thousand li all followed the crown prince; those beyond a thousand li sent their own crown princes, leading their ministers and subjects, all to the place where the Buddha was. They circumambulated the hall in mournful lamentation and made offerings of flowers and incense; those who arrived first withdrew first, and those who arrived later withdrew later.
The bhikṣus all asked Ānanda,
"What is the method for the funeral? He replied:

"When traveling eastward, thirty *li* from the city, there is a district in that land called Weizhi. There stand four crossroads with erected pillars and established shrines; the bricks are made of jade, each brick measuring three feet in length and breadth, while the stupa measures fifteen feet in length and breadth. The śarīra are contained within a golden jar placed precisely in the center. A stupa has been raised and a pillar erected, with silk banners suspended high above. Incense is burned and lamps are lit; the ground is swept clean and flowers are strewn. With the music of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, offerings are made morning and evening."
"The lay practitioners of the Śrī family should together construct a stūpa; Śakra, Brahmā, spirits, and nāgas, as well as kings, ministers, and subjects, shall escort the Buddha’s relics.
The lay practitioners respectfully assented, following Ānanda’s instructions.

Mahākāśyapa and the various arhats deliberated together with Aniruddha: "These three hundred thousand followers, along with the king, his ministers, and the common people, shall ultimately be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven in the presence of Maitreya."
When Maitreya attains Buddhahood, during his first discourse on the Dharma, ninety-six billion bhikṣus will attain arhatship. Maitreya shall then preach the sutra to sentient beings, saying:

"All those who possess these supernormal powers were those who built stupas during the time of Śākyamuni Buddha; they hung silk banners, burned incense, lit lamps, and practiced the Buddha's precepts—all of whom were pure laymen and pure laywomen."
Mahākāśyapa, along with Ānanda and the other arhats, deliberated together:
"When King Kūṭi reaches the end of his life, to what realm will he go?
Mahākāśyapa said:

"When this king’s life comes to an end, he shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; later, when Maitreya descends to become a Buddha, he shall be named Sudatta. He will construct a palace for Maitreya, establish a hall for preaching and receiving the Way, build a vihāra for the distribution of alms, and create a park for the solitary and the destitute; furthermore, he will provide robes, food, and medicine for the sick to support the community of bhikṣus."
Ānanda asked Mahākāśyapa:
"Why did the King of Kauśāmbī not attain the path of an arhat under Maitreya Buddha?
Mahākāśyapa replied:
"Because this king’s mind of desire has not yet grown weary of the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, and lamentation, he does not take up the path of the Arhat.
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda,
"Those who do not grow weary of the afflictions of birth and death shall never attain the Way."
Ānanda replied, "I have long been weary of this; why then have I not attained the Way?
Mahākāśyapa said:
"You need only uphold the precepts; do not merely contemplate the evils of the internal and external body, for you will continue to transmigrate through birth and death solely because of food.
When the eight bordering kingdoms heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa and that his relics were in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, they all raised armies and came to demand a portion of the relics.
The King of Kūyī said:
"The Buddha was in my kingdom and has now entered parinirvāṇa; I should have made offerings to him, yet you have traveled from afar at great hardship to visit us, and his śarīra cannot be obtained."
The eight kings replied:
"We join our palms and beg for a share of the relics; since you will not grant us any at all, we shall surely take them by force, even at the cost of our lives."

When the Heavenly Emperor saw the eight kings contending with one another, each desiring to obtain the relics to take back to their own kingdoms for veneration, he transformed himself into a Brahmin named Zhunqu. With palms joined, he stepped forward and exhorted the eight kings, saying: "Listen to my words.

While the Buddha was still in the world, you kings revered his honored teachings and were always compassionate and benevolent. As rulers of the people, it is not fitting that you should have such disputes. You ought to practice the four immeasurable minds and divide the Buddha’s relics so that every kingdom shall have a shrine. By opening the eyes of the blind and ignorant among the people, let them know there is a Buddha, establishing him as their ancestral lineage to ensure great and lasting blessings."
The devas, ghosts, dragons, kings, and common people all said:
"Excellent! Tuanqu!"
"He is the field of merit for all sentient beings.
Together they requested that the *tunqu* (the relics) be divided into eight equal portions.
The *tunqu* himself took a golden jar from heaven, lined its interior with rock honey (*śarkarā*), and having measured out the śarīra, he gave one jar to each person.

When the various kings obtained them, sorrow and joy welled up within them simultaneously; they all offered incense, flowers, suspended silks, variegated fabrics, burned incense, lit lamps, and performed music morning and evening.
Zhunqu knelt for a long time and begged for the remaining honey and *śarīra* in the jar, saying,
"I wish to establish a temple.
The kings granted them to him, and they subsequently entered the jar.
A Daoist named Huan Wei requested the śarīra from the king, who said, "They have already been divided and cannot be recovered;
there is only charred residue. Thereupon, he went to fetch it himself.
The Daoist took the charcoal and made offerings of incense and flowers.
Furthermore, a person from Cakravāḍa came to request the relics,
saying:
"It has already been divided;
there remains only ashes, which you may go and take yourself.
He then took the ashes and offered them for ninety days.
Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, and Kātyāyana deliberated together:

"Ānanda has followed the Buddha for the longest time and is uniquely close to him. Regarding the Buddha’s teachings and his vast, exemplary conduct, Ānanda has mastered them in his heart, illuminating every subtle detail. We should receive the Buddha’s laws and precepts from Ānanda and commit them in full detail to bamboo slips and silk."
The community of bhikṣus deliberated:
"Ānanda is still a layman; we fear he may have a covetous mind and conceal these sublime words, refusing to proclaim them in their entirety.
The community of bhikṣus said:
"You must deceive him.

Prepare a high seat for the assembly of holy elders; have the bhikṣu-saṃgha interrogate him three times with compassionate inquiry regarding his status as superior, middling, or inferior, and then ask about the essentials of the sūtras; in this way, you may obtain the truth."

The King of Kauśāmbī established Buddhist shrines, including meditation halls and retreat chambers, totaling three thousand in number. Within these, the bhikṣus resided, reciting the sūtras and practicing dhyāna. The king dispatched a minister named Mañju, leading three thousand soldiers, to provide constant guard over the Buddhist temples. Mahākāśyapa and Aniruddha together informed the community of bhikṣus that they must compile the Buddha’s sūtras and the Vinaya, which were termed the Four Āgamas.
Ānanda followed the Buddha as his most intimate disciple; because sentient beings were unrestrained in their lustful excesses, the Buddha composed one Āgama;
because they were violent, wrathful, and rebellious, he composed another Āgama;
and because they were ignorant and far removed from the correct path, he composed another Āgama.

He was unfilial toward his two parents, distanced himself from the worthy without honoring them, and having received the grace of the Buddha, he did not contemplate repaying it, yet instead composed an *Āgama*.
The assembly of śramaṇas said:
"Only Ānanda knows; indeed, the four *Āgamas* should have issued forth from Ānanda."
Mahākāśyapa said, "Ānanda was still a layman;
fearing he might have lingering attachments, he did not fully recite the scriptures.
The bhikṣus said:
"One may reprimand Ānanda for his previous conduct; we should place Ānanda upon a high seat, while the assembly of worthy ones remains below to inquire about the sūtras.
They all said, "Excellent!"
"This is truly most appropriate.

The administrative śramaṇa immediately assembled the holy assembly and expelled Ānanda. Once the holy assembly was all seated, he again commanded Ānanda to enter quickly. Upon entering, he prostrated himself in salutation before the holy assembly. Those who had attained arhatship remained seated as before, while those who had not yet attained it all rose.
The administrative śramaṇa led him to ascend the high seat in the center.
Ānanda declined, saying,
"This is not my seat."
The noble assembly all said, "Because of the Buddha’s sūtras, we honor you there; from you we shall receive the supreme Dharma of the Buddha.
Ānanda then sat down.
The assembly of the virtuous asked him:
"Do you know that you have seven transgressions?
When the World-Honored One was in the world, he said:"
"Within Jambudvīpa there is great joy;
why then do you remain silent?
The attendant śramaṇa called for Ānanda, and Ānanda immediately replied:
"Is the Buddha, the Unsurpassed, Truly Holy, and Noble One, not capable of acting with sovereign mastery?
Must he wait for my words?
Even if the Buddha were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, Maitreya, the Most Honored One, would still attain Buddhahood after him."
The noble assembly remained silent.
Ānanda was without fear.
The assembly of sages said in unison:
"Return to your seat for a moment; let us see if what you have proclaimed as the Dharma is identical to the True Dharma heard by the assembly.
Thus it was three times that Ānanda ascended, and three times he descended.
Ānanda spoke again, saying:
"Iyāmamustana, Iyāmamustana—this I have heard from the Buddha.
When the community of bhikṣus heard these words of Dharma from Ānanda, they were moved.
"Eyanmasudana, I have heard this from the Buddha.
They all choked with sobs and said,
"What are we to do about this!"
The Buddha had just passed into the world, yet now they further say, "I have heard from the Buddha that he spoke thus.
The devas, asuras, nāgas, kings, ministers, and commoners, as well as the fourfold assembly of disciples, all raised a cry of lamentation.

Mahākāśyapa selected forty Arhats from among the assembly of noble sages; from Ānanda, they received the four Āgamas. Each Āgama consisted of sixty rolls of silk. While the transcription of the scriptures was not yet complete, within the Buddha’s temple, four kinds of trees spontaneously grew: one tree was named Kacana, one was named Kapila, one was named Aśvattha, and one was named Nyagrodha.
The community of bhikṣus said:
"As we transcribed the four Āgamas with hearts of loving-kindness, four wondrous and divine trees spontaneously grew; for the four Āgamas are the Bodhi tree of the Buddha."

Thereupon, they made a mutual agreement to receive from the community of bhikṣus the two hundred and fifty pure and clear precepts; the bhikṣuṇī precepts consist of five hundred matters; the upāsaka precepts consist of five; and the upāsikā precepts consist of ten.

When the transcription of the sutras was completed, the assembly of bhikṣus each practiced the sutras and precepts, mutually transforming and instructing one another for a thousand years. Among them, those who maintained the precepts during these thousand years were destined to be in the presence of the fourth Buddha, Maitreya; the World-Honored One Maitreya shall then preach the Dharma to the devas.
He said:
"The assembly gathered here today are all those who observed the precepts during the time of Śākyamuni Buddha and have come to this summit.
Maitreya Buddha then spoke:
"You all must apply yourselves with diligence and exertion; the practices are difficult to fully master, so uphold as much as you can.

After the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, eight shrines were constructed: the ninth was the jar-stūpa (*kumbha-stūpa*), the tenth was the charcoal-stūpa (*aṅgāra-stūpa*), and the eleventh was the ash-stūpa (*bhasma-stūpa*).

The Sūtra says: The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month; on the eighth day he left his kingdom; on the eighth day he attained the Way; and on the eighth day he entered parinirvāṇa. At the time of the Puṣya asterism, he left home to study the Way; at the time of the Puṣya asterism, he attained the Way; and at the time of the Puṣya asterism, he passed into parinirvāṇa.
The grasses and trees once again blossomed with flowers and leaves, and the trees throughout the entire kingdom all became lush and flourishing.
When the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa*, the God among Gods of the three realms, his radiance was extinguished; yet throughout the ten directions, all beings turned back to take refuge in the Buddha.

The *Buddha-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll II: From the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until the eleventh day of the second month in the seventh year of Yongxing, a total of eight hundred and eighty-seven years and some months have passed; on the eleventh day of the seventh month.
Up to the current year of Bingxu, the total is nine hundred and fifteen years.
This is the record kept by the bhikṣu Kangri.
Furthermore, up to the sixth year of the Qingli era, the year of Bingxu, the cumulative total is one thousand nine hundred and ninety-four years.
